title: 7NEWS Spotlight: Pauline Hanson’s UK tour and meeting with Tommy Robinson exposes One Nation’s creative accounting on immigration numbers - 7NEWS
raw_text: Pauline Hanson has rarely had a better opportunity to get her facts right than in 7NEWS Spotlight’s special report broadcast on Sunday night. Months in production, with unprecedented access to Hanson, it included her first major television interview since calling for an Australian ‘monoculture’ at the National Press Club in June. The interview was conducted in London, by correspondent Liam Bartlett, midway through Hanson’s so-called fact-finding tour of the UK during which the Spotlight crew also filmed her meeting a who’s-who of Britain’s far right. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Hanson blames White Australia policy end for migration issues Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today Hanson claimed her trip provided both a warning and a political war plan for One Nation — to prevent Australia becoming the ‘sad sorry country’ she believes the UK now is. The anti-immigrant strategies she’s bringing home include a scheme for mass-deportation or ‘remigration’ drawn up by Restore Britain, which also proposes creating a ‘hostile environment’ for illegal immigrants — denying them welfare, housing, and health services to compel their voluntary expulsion. Heady stuff, if that’s where your politics run. Frightening if not. It may be 30 years since Hanson warned that Australia was in danger of ‘being swamped by Asians’ — but the message (read ‘Muslims’ for ‘Asians’) is the same. And so are the alarming statistics offered in support. But numbers that can be shouted from the fringes without regard for the facts require much greater scrutiny when the shouter commands up to 30 per cent of the popular vote and is jockeying for post of preferred Prime Minister. On a podcast with British far-right extremist Tommy Robinson, filmed ‘fly-on-the-wall’ by Spotlight, Hanson claimed Australia was taking in 739,000 migrants a year. “Every 59 seconds,” she told Robinson, “we got a new migrant in Australia.” If numbers were words, 739,000 would be a weasel. The year Hanson is quoting (2022-23), was the first post-COVID statistic, with a large catch-up factor of Australians caught abroad, family reunions postponed, and foreign students returning. But what makes the number even harder to pin down is that Hanson fails to mention the 219,000 people who left Australia in the same year. That record catch-up year added 518,000 to Australia’s population — not 739,000. And the number has fallen every year since. In 2025 it was just 301,000 — far less than half what the senator told Robinson. The $20 million Cotswolds manor of former Neighbours star Holly Valance, dubbed “radical-right royalty” by the British tabloids, is an unlikely place for earnest consideration of mass deportation. But, invited in, the Spotlight team was rolling as Rupert Lowe, founder and leader of Restore Britain, handed Hanson his party’s manifesto mapping a plan to expel nearly two million people from the UK within three years. “Pauline, I’d like to give you this,” he said. “This is a jewel of what you need to do in Australia.” A man whose far-right ideology is somewhat at odds with his crumpled country-gentleman manner, could have easily followed it up with “and please pass the sugar.” Hanson’s reply: “We’re very much on the same page.” Spotlight later confirmed her commitment. “Do you think Senator, this concept of mass deportation is a good one?” Hanson was asked. “Oh, I love it,” she replied. Lowe’s claim of nearly two million illegal immigrants in the UK is at least twice the most widely cited estimate of Britain’s illegal population. But who, in Hanson’s monocultural nation, would be in her Australian mass-deportation queue? Riding through Luton’s Muslim quarter with Robinson, she put the number at 100,000: people who “get off the airplane, destroy their identification... overstay their visas and play refugees.” The Senator’s clear suggestion — and Robinson’s even clearer assumption as they traded disparaging quips about the prevalence of women in burkas and niqabs outside the car window — was that the majority of her ‘100,000’ are in the vanguard of radical Islam. With the brevity of truth, the real number is 77,700 who stayed on after their visas expired or were cancelled, led by citizens of China, Malaysia and the US. Not one of the top three groups is from the Middle East. The typical “illegal” is not a boat arrival or a black-flag radical, it’s someone who flew in on a student or tourist visa and simply never went home. If her mass deportees are ever lined up, the third-largest contingent will be Americans. There was similar arithmetic throughout Spotlight’s behind-the-scenes coverage of Hanson’s UK tour. She told Nigel Farage’s treasury spokesman — Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick — that one imperative for removing ‘illegal’ immigrants from Australia was that “we’ve got 150,000 people that are living in cars, tents. We can’t provide the housing for them.” The closest official figure relating to that claim is in the last Australian Census, which tallied 7636 people in tents, improvised dwellings or sleeping rough. That’s one-twentieth of the Hanson homeless. When Robinson discussed the number of Muslims in Australia with Hanson — “you’ve got about 4 per cent... that’s a million? — she replied “they do breed.” In fact, Muslim families on average have three children — and the number is falling. Mark Twain wrote (quoting English statesman Benjamin Disraeli): “There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics.” Disraeli — twice prime minister and three times Britain’s treasurer — was a canny politician who clearly knew the power of numbers to convince. Hanson is a perhaps pale, but fervent, imitator. The Spotlight report captured an unguarded Hanson amidst a likeminded coterie, who share her innumerate approach to immigration statistics. All her numbers run the same way. Away from the truth. Stream free on

title: Amanda Rishworth and Nat Barr clash over tradie ranking in skilled migration scheme - 7NEWS
raw_text: Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth has refused to say whether tradies should be prioritised over economists and animal trainers under Australia’s skilled migration scheme, despite the country’s housing crisis. The minister was grilled by Sunrise host Nat Barr over the government’s migration priorities on Wednesday and was pressed on why construction workers remain in the same priority tier as a range of other occupations despite Australia’s desperate need for more homes. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Tradies ranked equal to actors in migration scheme Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today Under the current Skilled Migration Scheme, nurses and health professionals are listed in tier one, teachers sit in tier two, while construction trades are ranked in tier three alongside occupations including actors, dancers, economists, animal handlers, and animal trainers. Rishworth defended the government’s approach, saying it had significantly increased the number of construction workers entering Australia. “We’ve had three times increase in the number of construction workers since we’ve come to government taking up those jobs,” she said. “But importantly, we’re also fast-tracking the recognition of those skills. So not only can those construction workers come here, but they can actually work on construction sites.” Rishworth said an additional 20,000 people had their skills recognised through the fast-tracking measures, allowing them to begin working sooner. However, when Barr repeatedly asked whether tradies should continue to be ranked alongside occupations such as animal trainers and actors, the minister stopped short of giving a direct answer. “I want to see more tradies, I want to see more doctors, I want to see more nurses, people that we need, and of course what we’ve had is the opposition play a very sneaky game of talking down our skilled migration, telling us that skilled migration isn’t important but not being clear about who they would cut,” she said. “What I would say is that when it comes to making sure we’ve got more construction workers in the country, I absolutely support that and I also want to see those skills recognised… so they can get to work quickly.” Shadow Defence Minister James Patterson accused the government of failing to prioritise the workers Australia needs most during the housing crisis. “Only a Labor government, which is beholden to corrupt unions like the CFMEU, would think, in the middle of our worst-ever housing crisis, that they [animal trainers and actors] are equally important to bring to Australia right now,” he said. “Labor thinks that we should bring in as many economists and actors as we should bring in sparkies and carpenters and plumbers and other critical trades.” Rishworth rejected Patterson’s claim that unions were influencing the government’s migration settings, arguing the tier system had not changed since the previous Coalition government. Barr immediately challenged the explanation. “Why not?” she asked. “We’ve got a housing crisis now, so why hasn’t it changed in four years?” Rishworth again declined to directly address why tradies remain in the same migration priority tier, instead saying the government continues to receive expert advice on skilled occupation lists. title: Pauline Hanson meets with UK far-right figure Tommy Robinson - 7NEWS
raw_text: Pauline Hanson has met with UK far-right figure Tommy Robinson to record a new podcast interview. Robinson, 43, took to social media to share news of their sit-down, and what is to come. “Had a fascinating time chatting to one of the bravest lady’s (sic) on the planet,” the controversial activist shared on X. “Fearless, relentless, consistent, fighting for the Australian people and hopefully the next leader of her nation. Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today “Podcast coming soon...” Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, founded the far-right Islamophobic group the English Defence League in 2009. He has multiple criminal convictions and has previously been denied a visa to visit Australia. Just last month, he appeared on an episode of The Karl Stefanovic Show to talk about “free speech, censorship, immigration and the direction he believes Britain should be heading in”. The interview was removed from online platforms and led to Stefanovic’s high-profile exit from Nine. It was later reuploaded to Hanson’s Please Explain account. “Tommy Robinson has a lesson for Australians,” the account said. “If we don’t learn from the UK’s mistakes on immigration and radical Islam, we are going to face the same destruction. “This is exactly what Karl was trying to bring to Australia’s attention.” News of the Hanson-Robinson podcast episode comes after the One Nation leader enjoyed a drink with former Neighbours star Holly Valance. “Nothing like a beer with your mate at the pub on a hot day,” the soap star posted online, sharing a picture from ex-Top Gear presenter Jeremy Clarkson’s pub in the UK. The Senator’s Please Explain Account said Valance had been a longtime supporter of “true conservatives”. “While here in England, I took some time out to catch up with Holly Valance who has been a staunch backer of true conservatives both here in the UK and myself in Australia,” the post read. “Some big meetings lined up this week. I’ll have more to say about those discussions later in the week.” Stream free on

title: WA’s multibillion-dollar grain harvest at risk as workers blocked or delayed - 7NEWS
raw_text: There are fears a bumper multibillion-dollar harvest in WA is at risk because of a new crackdown on backpacker and temporary visas. An army of workers arrive to help on the land every year but farmers say they are now being blocked or delayed in a bureaucratic nightmare. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Visa delays threaten WA’s bumper harvest season Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today “Farmers are distressed trying to work out who’s going to operate all their big machinery this year,” farmer Mic Fels told 7NEWS. The Esperance farmer says the Federal Government’s decision to slow down approvals is another blow to the industry. “We have three Danish skilled farm workers, they’ve got university qualifications, they’ve got years of experience operating exactly the same machines that we own,” he said. “They’re sitting on hold — have been since July — waiting for their visas to be processed.” Harvest has made an earlier than expected start in WA, and grain farmers are eyeing off a crop of 23 million tonnes. A visa approval which used to be just days or even minutes can now take up to three months. “It’s like they’re picking on farmers now,” Fels said. “Farmers have had to deal with a lot this year. “There’s been the risk over whether there was going to be fertiliser, whether there was going to be diesel. “We got through that, but the uncertainty is the big cause of stress, and now it’s the uncertainty over workforce.” National Farmers Federation vice president John Hassell said working holidaymakers “stay in accommodations on farms” and “don’t put pressure on all those sorts of things”. “I think this is a very ill-informed response to calls by One Nation and the Liberal Party to reduce immigration,” he said. The federal government has now agreed to fast track some urgent visa requests but approvals are not guaranteed and farmers say time is already slipping away. “Every day that a harvest is delayed, it decreases the value and the quality of the crops,” Hassell said. title: Military called in as more than 40,000 migrants from Morocco pour into Spanish border territory - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: Spanish officials say more than 40,000 people crossed from Morocco into Spain, via the North African enclave of Ceuta. Footage showed hundreds of migrants swimming from the Moroccan side, and others breaking through a gate on land. What's next? At least 18 people died during the crossing and Spanish government has deployed military units to reinforce police at the border. Spanish military units are being deployed to reinforce police in the city of Ceuta after migrants in Morocco broke through fences, overwhelming the local force. Spain's interior ministry estimates more than 40,000 people swam, with 18 people declared dead from the process. Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers association representing Civil Guard officers, said some migrants drowned in the crossing, and some are believed to have been killed in the stampede exiting the water. Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain, on the North African coast, and has been the scene of previous mass migration events in recent years. Ceuta, on the northern African coast, would be a 5-kilometre swim from the Moroccan town of Fnideq. Video footage showed hundreds of migrants swimming or floating on inner tubes from the Moroccan side, and others breaking through a gate on land and running into the city. "It was very tough. The police tried to stop us. But our will and determination allowed us to come here," migrant Jadid Zacaria, his hair and shirt still wet from the ocean, said in an interview as migrants streamed through a border gate nearby. Nine people were found dead, local authorities said, adding to a toll of 60 migrants who have died attempting to cross into Ceuta in recent months. The Spanish government said 200 specialised police officers and 60 troops had arrived from the Spanish mainland to reinforce the enclave's regular forces. The scene was reminiscent of 2021, when about 10,000 people from Morocco and sub-Saharan Africa, many of them minors, entered the enclave of 85,000 people in days. Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez will travel to Ceuta today with Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska for meetings with security forces and local authorities, his office said. Morocco's Interior Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 'Entering from the sea' Earlier, a Guardia Civil spokesperson said migrants were "massively entering from the sea" around the Tarajal breakwater, a border seawall that migrants can swim around to enter Ceuta. The spokesperson said police were overwhelmed. Many local shops were shuttered. Enrique Serrano, who runs a women's clothing store in central Ceuta, said business owners were organising self-defence because they believed police resources would be insufficient. "I'm not opening this afternoon because the situation is extremely tense … The first thing I have to do is protect my business and my family," he said. Ceuta and Melilla — another Spanish autonomous city located in North Africa — have the European Union's only land borders with Africa. Both cities periodically experience surges in attempted crossings by migrants seeking to reach Europe. Local government seeks state of emergency Spain's Socialist government stands out in Europe for its pro-migrant stance, and it has recently launched a program to provide legal status for some 500,000 undocumented migrants, triggering an influx of applications double that number. Right-wing parties criticised the drive, arguing it would attract more migrants to Spain, and were quick to blame Mr Sanchez for allowing the situation in Ceuta to reach crisis proportions. Conservative opposition People's Party leader Alberto Nuñez Feijoo said in a post on X: "The situation in Ceuta is desperate. The government cannot look the other way… because we are facing a national security crisis." Ceuta Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas had urged the national government to declare an emergency over the mass arrivals. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on X that the images from Ceuta showed that Mr Sanchez's migration policy was "misguided". A source told Reuters that Italy was exploring reintroducing border controls for people travelling from Spain to Italy, which normally falls in the European Union's passport-free Schengen zone. 'An explosion' Earlier this month, Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants intercepted at sea while attempting to reach Ceuta or Melilla could not be summarily returned under the enclaves' special "border rejection" regime, which allows authorities to immediately send back people caught crossing the border fences. Spain's government said it was the "exploitation by mafias and criminal organisations" of this ruling that had triggered the migrant surge, not its bid to give legal status to some undocumented migrants. Loading... "It has been a slow trickle since the Supreme Court's ruling, but today has been an explosion," the Guardia Civil spokesperson told Reuters. The Interior Ministry said it was working closely with Morocco to address the surge in irregular arrivals, having prevented thousands of migrants from illegally entering Ceuta in recent days. Migrant rights activist Zakaria Zarroqui said people were still flocking to the adjacent Moroccan city of Fnideq in an attempt to cross into Ceuta and the situation was still out of control. Mauricio Valiente, director of the Spanish Commission for Refugees, which has lawyers working in Ceuta, said the migrants crossing into the enclave were of Moroccan and sub-Saharan origin, including families. Reuters / AP / AFP

title: How Pauline Hanson's winning the migration debate - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: Two months since Pauline Hanson's Press Club address calling for monoculturalism in Australia, new polling shows more Australians prefer her stance on immigration than that of either of the major parties. Today, Tony Barry, a former Liberal party strategist and director at Redbridge Group on One Nation's appeal. New polling this week shows more Australians prefer her stance on immigration than that of either of the two major parties. Today Tony Barry, a former Liberal Party strategist and director at Redbridge Group, on One Nation's appeal. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Tony, you've been involved in politics, well, for a pretty long time now. And so you know that immigration has always been a touchstone issue for voters, hasn't it? Tony Barry: Yeah, immigration is always an issue that animates voters. And in the current political environment, we've got cost of living pressures, but also housing affordability, whether it be renting or buying. And in the era where politicians like Pauline Hanson readily identify as grievance, you have this perfect storm brewing. Sam Hawley: Yeah, but I mean, you kind of think back to the Howard years, it was sort of key to his leadership because who can really forget, "we will decide who comes to this country." John Howard, former Prime Minister: We have a proud record of welcoming people from 140 different nations, but we will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come. Tony Barry: Yeah, the 2001 election was fairly unique insofar as we had September 11 earlier in that year, and then shortly after that, Tampa. News report: Well, it's been a day of high drama on the high seas. A Norwegian freighter carrying more than 400 mainly Afghani asylum seekers has been refused entry to Australia and is still anchored 70 kilometres from Christmas Island. Tony Barry: And so that spoke to sovereignty and the key value there that was driving vote considerations was sovereignty. But now in the current environment, we have had record numbers of immigration post COVID and there's reasons for that. And we've done a lot of polling on this. And one of the reasons why people are voting One Nation is because of what they describe as Pauline Hanson's authenticity. The fact that she has been talking about these issues for so long. And there's a political reward for that. Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader: At the centre of this crisis is the utterly flawed policy of multiculturalism. We cannot be a multicultural society. We are a multiracial society, but we must be monocultural. Sam Hawley: So, Pauline Hanson and One Nation, they're ensuring, I suppose, that immigration, the issue of immigration and debate around it is gaining traction again. The art of politics is to control the narrative. Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader: I'm always listening. And that's why my policy to slash immigration reflects what most Australians want. Tony Barry: I think in the case of immigration, because of Hanson's strong lead, and she has on our polling a 40% of voters say she is the best person to handle that issue. That is the art of politics is playing to your strengths. Sam Hawley: All right, well, Tony, let's consider then why it is that voters feel this way, why they like what Pauline Hanson has to say on immigration. What exactly is One Nation's policies on immigration? It's not actually that clear, is it? Tony Barry: Well, for a lot of voters, she's the anti-establishment candidate. And we asked One Nation voters in our last poll, why? Why are you voting One Nation? And of course, at the moment, it's around 30% of the electorate. So it's a very significant number. For about 16% of those currently supporting One Nation, they say it's because Hanson represents change, and they want change. For another 16% of those One Nation voters, it's their anti-establishment credentials. They're sick and tired of the major parties. For another 14% say they think she's authentic. And 11% say it's her immigration policy. And a lot of it is not so much because of immigration per se, although that is a component, it's that they feel the current political model isn't working for them, and they want to smash it up. Sam Hawley: So not so much the nitty gritty of the immigration policy. That's not really on voters' minds. But if you go to their website, the party says it would cap visas at 130,000 per year. Now if it did that, that would lead to zero or even negative migration. I don't know that voters understand that. Tony Barry: And I think that's the point. I think that a lot of voters don't understand that because Labor, they control the microphone. And yet I'm not really sure what their immigration policy is. Now I'm a high volume user of media. And if I don't understand what their objectives are, then I think you'll find most voters also don't understand. And I think there's been a failing of both sides to explain the importance of immigration, particularly skilled immigration. John Howard, as you mentioned before, actually increased immigration, and he changed it from family reunion and skewed it more towards skilled. And he explained why that was important. About 10% of the healthcare workforce in Australia are migrants. So there's been a failing of the major parties, particularly the government at the moment, to explain why good immigration program is important for Australia. In that environment, it's very easy for an anti-establishment party like One Nation to undermine the credentials of that campaign. Sam Hawley: Yeah. All right. Well, Barnaby Joyce, he was asked about this 130,000 figure. He said it really only applies to the net intake of migrants. Pauline Hanson, she was grilled about it on News 24, formerly Sky's Sunday Agenda. Again, not clear at all. News24 journalist: What's your permanent number? What permanent number do you want to see here? Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader: Well, I want to see 130,000 as the permanent number that are here. So there are people, look, there's people that come in, they come in on visas. So we have the palm workers, we have backpackers, we have short term workers. If you've been here for over 14 months or 16 months, you're basically classified can be a permanent into the country. Yeah. But we've allowed people... Pauline, sorry News24 journalist: to interrupt. I just want to clarify this. Sam Hawley: But as you say, we also had this issue with Tony Burke, right? He was meant to have this major address at the National Press Club. He cancelled it. So really, as you say, voters are not really clear where they stand with any of these parties. Tony Barry: Yeah, I think that was obviously a very untidy episode for Tony Burke having to cancel it. But I think he made the right decision strategically because you've got to get these things right. And rather than sort of going in and sort of walking it back and then having this sort of very convoluted position, they've basically caught their breath. They're obviously going to try and recalibrate and then do some positioning on it. Because at the moment, that's a really important issue for them to neutralise. Because whilst only fifth most salient issue on voters' hierarchy, the more you talk about an issue and the more oxygen it gets, then it has the potential to increase in salience. And Labor would be very concerned about that. They can't afford to be trailing or not competitive in the issues that voters will consider when they go into mark their ballot card. Sam Hawley: Yeah, the ABC reported that Tony Burke, he had postponed that speech because the cabinet couldn't agree on the detail. But what you're saying is really what the government and Labor wants to do here is, well, come up with some figure for immigration that neutralises this issue or neutralises the topic as an issue. Tony Barry: Yeah, and also they've got to pre-position their policy. You know, the great failing of many policies in governments, whether it be Labor or Coalition, is a failure to sort of execute the idea. You just sort of drop it on the table like a raw piece of steak and you expect voters to digest it. You do need to position these policies. Sam Hawley: All right, and what about the Coalition? How does it play into all of this? The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, he seems to want to link new houses to net migration. Angus Taylor, Opposition leader: A coalition will cap immigration numbers based on the number of homes constructed each year. Hear, hear. Never again will a government be able to bring in more people than our housing can support. Hear, hear. That's our commitment. Tony Barry: Well, I think the problem for the Coalition at the moment is their primary vote is so low, they're not even in the conversation. Their job strategically is to get over the top of One Nation, so you can't win when you're coming third. There's just no universe where they're going to be competitive with the primary vote in the low 20s. Sam Hawley: All right, well, Tony, as you mentioned, One Nation seems to be elevating the issue of immigration. So do you think that is a tactic that will be successful and beneficial to the party in the end when it comes to election time? Tony Barry: A lot of it's going to depend on how the two traditional major parties respond and are they able to communicate differentiated policies on salient issues. And there's no more salient issue than cost of living and housing and healthcare. So if they can articulate an agenda that voters can digest and believe in, then I think they'll effectively neutralise One Nation. How do you control the One Nation vote? You look back at the Howard government. In 2004, One Nation did not win a cent spot. In fact, the coalition won four Senate seats, including a newcomer at the time, Barnaby Joyce, and the coalition won four, which is unprecedented for a major party to win four out of six Senate spots in a half Senate election. But such was the success of Howard and Costello on a macro level and the late Ron Boswell on the ground arguing against One Nation that they were able to basically neutralise One Nation as a political force. But a large part of that was that under the Howard government at the time, wage growth was around 24.6% and interest rates generally fell one or two points or more every year. And so there wasn't as much grievance in the electorate because people were quite happy. And the greatest measurement of that is we always ask a diagnostic test. Do you think Australia is heading in the right direction or the wrong direction? Now, I remember polling in 2007, the right direction was 65%. 65% of Australians said we're heading in the right direction. And the most recent poll we did for the Fin Review, 54% said we're heading in the wrong direction. So there's been a significant shift over the last 19 years in people's assessments of how the country is travelling, and that's building the grievance. And that is why One Nation is able to identify that grievance and speak to that grievance. Sam Hawley: And it's got hold of the narrative and it's driving it, right? And that counts for a lot. That's what every political party wants to do. Tony Barry: Exactly. Exactly. You want to control the microphone because you get to drive the narrative and the opposition typically responds. But Hanson is in the position where in some cases she actually drives the narrative and the government is responding and the opposition is responding.

title: Labor was poised to reveal massive migration cuts, then suddenly delayed - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has postponed a scheduled appearance at the National Press Club. He was set to unveil sweeping cuts to migration, which the ABC understands were internally contentious. What's next? The speech is to be rescheduled. A spokesperson for the minister said the decision was made because some details would not be finalised in time. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has postponed a speech at the National Press Club where he was expected to unveil far-reaching changes to Australia's migration settings in a bid to quell public anger and growing support for One Nation. Mr Burke was due to appear tomorrow but withdrew yesterday afternoon. A government source said the speech would be rescheduled in the near future. A spokesperson for the minister told the ABC the speech would "deal with the migration system as a whole". "Yesterday it became clear that some elements of the speech would not be finalised by Thursday. We're working with the press club to find a new date," the spokesperson said. Three sources familiar with the government's thinking told the ABC the minister had been preparing a package of measures to achieve a quick and drastic cut to net migration. It is understood the proposal was considered by cabinet on Monday. Among the measures canvassed were tougher family visa rules, a cap on the number of backpackers in the country and restrictions on the work and appeal rights of asylum seekers. Several sources said internal deliberations had been highly contentious. One senior government source downplayed the extent of internal disagreements and said the elements that were yet to be finalised were minor, but confirmed that the changes would be wide-ranging and designed to give the government greater control over net migration figures. The government has endured sustained criticism from One Nation and the Coalition since a post-pandemic spike in net migration, which exceeded half a million people in 2023. That figure tracks arrivals and departures of both Australians and migrants. The spike was caused in part by a glut of demand which had accumulated during the pandemic, when migration was effectively halted, and also because of pandemic-era measures to encourage migrants who were already in Australia to stay for longer. Before the 2025 federal election, the Albanese government moved to restrict international student numbers. Net overseas migration has fallen to just over 300,000 on the latest figures, but has repeatedly exceeded Treasury projections. Net migration is hard for governments to control because most of the temporary visa categories are driven by demand and not formally limited. Many of the policy suggestions understood to form part of Mr Burke's package would give the government more control over that number, at least in the short term. Quiet changes leading up to speech Last month, Mr Burke quietly made a series of changes likely to further reduce net migration. They included a substantial across-the-board increase in visa application fees, which was never formally announced but seems to have been decided in the early months of this year, and took effect on July 1. Budget papers published in May showed the budget would collect an extra $1.2 billion in visa fees this financial year alone, compared to what had been forecast in the December mid-year budget update, and equating to an increase of 24 per cent. Mr Burke also made two ministerial directives, ordering officials to prioritise onshore applicants over offshore applicants for permanent skilled and family visas. There were limited exceptions for those working in law enforcement and defence. The direction to prioritise one pile of applicants over another is a similar strategy to the one the government deployed to reduce the number of international students. Given the large backlog of applications, it effectively amounts to a short-term pause for applicants who are de-prioritised, which would in turn reduce the number of overseas arrivals. Further sweeping changes expected Mr Burke's proposed reform package was also expected to prevent the spouses, children and parents of Australian citizens and permanent residents from applying for family visas while they are in the country as tourists. This has been a common approach for many families seeking to stay together in Australia while they wait for their permanent visas to be approved. Australian law requires that permanent family visas be granted to all those who apply, provided they meet the criteria. title: PM rules out British backpackers being forced to work in regions - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The government was considering imposing regional work requirements on British backpackers to make the scheme less attractive in a bid to bring down migration numbers. The prime minister has publicly poured cold water on that idea, heading off a diplomatic stoush. What's next? No date has been set for the government to unveil its changes in migration policy after Tony Burke postponed a National Press Club address earlier this month. The prime minister has vowed not to make British backpackers work in regional areas as part of a looming migration overhaul, defusing a potential diplomatic stoush with the United Kingdom. British citizens on Working Holiday Maker, or backpacker, visas are allowed to live in Australia for up to three years without any specific work requirements under a free trade deal which came into force in 2023. Working holiday makers from all other countries must work in regional or remote areas to have their visas extended beyond a year. The favourable treatment has led to a steep increase in the number of UK backpackers coming to Australia, up from 47,238 in 2023/24 to 79,412 in 2024/25 according to Home Affairs data. Under pressure to clamp down on temporary visas and reduce overseas arrivals, the government was considering a plan to impose regional work requirements on British backpackers to make the scheme less attractive. But some in the government were concerned that would clearly breach the free trade agreement between Australia and the United Kingdom at a time when the government had positioned itself as an international champion for trade rules. Anthony Albanese quashed the proposal on Wednesday afternoon, ruling out any changes to the deal. "The UK situation is a separate agreement as a result of the UK free trade agreement which we are certainly honouring," Mr Albanese said. He intervened not long after UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on the sidelines of a Five Eyes meeting in Sydney. After that meeting, Mr Burke did not deny the issue had been canvassed. "We talk regularly about all migration issues, about the issues we are managing in each of our countries," Mr Burke told reporters in Sydney. "In terms of anything coming forward, as to any changes we'd made to the migration program, those are decisions that would be made by the Australian cabinet." The possible change to UK arrangements was one of several under consideration as part of a wider crackdown on immigration which Mr Burke was due to announce three weeks ago before being forced to postpone. No new date has been set for the policy announcement, which is designed to ensure Labor meets its own target of cutting net overseas migration (NOM) from the current 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028. Backpackers are a significant contributor to the NOM with a record 321,116 visas being issued last year, up from 234,556 the year before. Mr Burke last month paused the processing of applications from 24 countries including Argentina, Chile, Spain, Poland, Thailand and Malaysia, and pushed workers applying for overseas skilled visas to the back of the queue. "The processing of backpacker visas across the entire program is happening more slowly than it was," Mr Burke said. "And similarly there are changes we've made to the permanent program in preferencing, at the moment, onshore positions rather than offshore." The far-reaching directive is designed to stop, or dramatically slow, the number of overseas arrivals but has created an enormous amount of confusion and concern within the business, hospitality and tourism sectors which rely on migrant workers. As one business figure told the ABC, "everything has ground to a halt". One Nation and the Coalition are promising dramatic cuts to migration, but both have ruled out any cuts to backpacker visas given their popularity in regional areas.

title: One Nation MP leaves door open to slashing citizens' family visas - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: One Nation MP David Farley says his party is open to cutting visas for family members of Australian citizens. On Monday, One Nation unveiled its policy to reduce Australia's temporary migration intake by 750,000 people over three years, including a ban on families of temporary skilled workers and international students. What's next? Mr Farley said One Nation had commissioned "extensive" economic modelling of its migration plan and would reveal more of the party's immigration strategy. One Nation MP David Farley has left the door open to "potentially" cutting visas for family members of Australian citizens, as the party prepares to reveal more details of its immigration plan within coming weeks. Mr Farley said whether the party considered preventing citizens from bringing family members to Australia to live would be dependent on the availability of services, including housing. "It's a hypothetical question, but can we grow our health system, our education system and other infrastructure we need to make sure the existing population that's here … are not under pressure?" he told the ABC. On Monday One Nation revealed its plan to reduce Australia's temporary migration intake by 750,000 places over three years, partly by barring the families of temporary skilled migrants and international students from entering the country. Mr Farley, who previously stated One Nation's migration policy would be "not too different" to Labor's, rejected suggestions that cutting family visas would deter the skilled migrants needed to plug critical workforce shortages from coming to Australia in the first place. "It is 2026. People have the ability now to work remotely … the reaches of the world are all 12 or 14 hours on a flight, and ultimately in an employment contract of skilled labour, everything is negotiable," he said. The minor party did not detail what its permanent migration intake would be, but Mr Farley said its immigration plan would be rolled out "completely" within the next fortnight. Caps on family visa intake 'illegal' Former deputy secretary of the Immigration Department Abul Rizvi said it would be illegal to cap family visas issued for Australian citizens. Despite that, Labor's current intake of permanent family visas is limited to 52,460 per year. "Under section 87 of the migration act, the government doesn't have the legal power to cap visas for the partners and dependent children of Australian citizens and permanent residents," Mr Rizvi said. "Regardless, successive governments have administratively — and illegally — limited the number of such visas issued." Mr Rizvi said, as a result, the backlog of partner visa applications was now about 120,000 and growing. "None of the parties have indicated what they will do about this illegal behaviour," he said. The government has been contacted for comment. One Nation to reveal 'complete' migration policy Meanwhile, One Nation is also facing calls to reveal the economic impact of its proposal to send Australia into "net negative migration" for three years. Labor frontbencher Murray Watt said the plan would destroy regional economies and likely send Australian into recession, while Shadow Immigration Minister Jonno Duniam demanded to see the party's costings. Mr Farley said One Nation had commissioned "extensive" economic modelling of its migration plan. "We've done the modelling and we will roll our strategy out on immigration completely over the next fortnight," he said. Weeks after Immigration Minister Tony Burke was forced to shelve a speech in which he was expected to unveil sweeping changes to Labor's migration settings, pressure is mounting on the government to unveil its policy to the Australian public. "I think they're going to be two years too late, but it's critical," Mr Rizvi said. "Part of the reason for One Nation's strength is because the government has failed to explain its policies, and the merit of those policies, to the Australian public." Senator Duniam said the Coalition would release its policy, with full costings, within weeks.

title: Love when you don't know when you'll meet again - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: After Mohammad "Mo" Mohammadi's brother died in 2020, he wanted to honour his memory with a portrait. That's when he came across Iran-based artist Fereshteh Ahmadi on Instagram. He never expected that a simple message would lead to a love story shaped by distance, war and agonising immigration struggles. These are Mo's words. Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us. After I reached out to Fereshteh on Instagram, she told her father. He recognised my name. It turned out we were from the same village in Afghanistan, and our families had been neighbours. It was a complete coincidence. We were both Afghan refugees who had ended up in Iran; Fereshteh's father had fled there many years before, and it was in Iran he got married and started his family. I had moved to Iran with my uncle as a young child. Throughout 2021, Fereshteh and I spoke on Instagram, and we quickly became friends. Fereshteh offered to send the artwork she'd drawn of my brother to me in Australia. I'd relocated there in 2010. But I was already planning to visit Iran the following year and wanted to collect it from her in person. When we met in real life, I could instantly feel she was a really nice person. When you find the other half of yourself, you just know Soon after that first meeting, we decided to get engaged. We had a little party with our families and got our marriage certificate from the Embassy of Afghanistan in Tehran in 2022. Five weeks later, I had to return to Australia for work. We were hoping to get a visa for Fereshteh to join me. But because she's an Afghan refugee in Iran, it's difficult for her to get the paperwork she needs. I had no idea when we would see each other again, so a few years ago, I asked Fereshteh to send me some of her artworks in the mail. I didn't tell her what I wanted them for, but I submitted them to a local art gallery in Bordertown, South Australia, where I now live. They all sold. People really loved them, and even asked for commissioned works. Fereshteh was really excited about all the support and used the money to purchase new art supplies. It's been almost three years now since we last saw each other in person We miss each other a lot. We're really just at the start of our relationship, and we should be spending time together. I was planning to visit Fereshteh earlier this year, but the week before I was due to depart, Israel and the US attacked Iran. My flight was cancelled, and I could not go. When the conflict started, I lost contact with Fereshteh for nearly two months. No phone calls, no text messages, no nothing. I had no idea where Fereshteh and her family were, or what they were going to do. It was really hard. I was always thinking about her and what was going to happen. Were they going to get bombed? Were the missiles going to drop directly where they were? Once the internet was restored, Fereshteh and her family texted me saying they were OK. I was really, really happy to hear that they were safe, at least. There was nothing I could do, because there were no flights, and everything was closed. Thankfully, Fereshteh and I can speak often now, but the internet is very poor, and we cannot video call. Still, at least we can talk. She's alright, and her family's alright. Loading... Still, we're hopeful about our future together My dream is to meet Fereshteh back in Iran so we can do the ceremony and celebrate with our families, before returning to Australia. Then we can finally build our lives together, and hopefully have children some day. I hope that she continues with her art when she arrives in Australia. But I'll support her with whatever she wants to be or become. She might want to study, or maybe even teach her own art class. In Australia, she'll have the freedom to do that. In Iran, she can't study or go to university. She can't work, and she can't even sell her artworks. It's too difficult, especially with the conflict happening now. I've bought a house in Bordertown, and it's like home to me, so I hope she'll like it here too. I can't wait to be together again, going out for dinner, going for holidays — even going camping. title: Hundreds of migrants flood into Spain’s Ceuta exclave from Morocco - News.com.au
raw_text: Hundreds of migrants flood into Spain's Ceuta exclave from Morocco Madrid said on Thursday it would despatch soldiers to Ceuta to ensure security after hundreds of migrants entered Spain's north African exclave from neighbouring Morocco and hundreds more headed there. The Spanish government's delegation in the enclave told AFP that the bodies of nine migrants who died while trying to reach Ceuta by swimming had been recovered. Migration from Morocco into Spain's two north African territories, Ceuta and Melilla, has long been a politically sensitive issue between the two countries, as thousands cross the border at times. Italy called on Thursday for Spain to be suspended from Europe's open-borders Schengen zone, prompting a backlash from Spain, which summoned the Italian envoy to Madrid. AFP reporters saw a stream of adults and children, most of them soaked, entering the town of Ceuta after having swum there. Discarded flotation rings and clothes were discarded on the shore near where the border barrier meets the sea. "The armed forces will reinforce the Civil Guard in the exercise of its powers and any others that may be necessary to maintain security in the city of Ceuta," Spain's interior ministry said. It did not specify how many soldiers would be sent to the small territory of 18.5 square kilometres (seven square miles) but said the Civil Guard's strength there would be nearly doubled from the current level of 80. It will also send diving teams and coastguard ships. - Spain 'profoundly wrong' - Italy said on Thursday Spain should be suspended from the Schengen zone -- a system of open borders spanning 29 European countries that have officially abolished controls at their common borders. "I am in favour of closing the Schengen area with Spain," Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani wrote on X. "Irregular and uncontrolled immigration poses a danger to national security," he claimed. "The images coming from Ceuta show how the Madrid government's decision to grant Spanish, and therefore European, citizenship to over 500,000 irregular immigrants is profoundly wrong and encourages human trafficking," he argued. title: ‘Wild’: Shock as Aussie visa fees skyrocket - News.com.au
raw_text: ‘Wild’: Shock as Aussie visa fees skyrocket for students, backpackers and Kiwis International students, backpackers and Kiwis have hit out at “wild” visa fee increases of nearly 200 per cent which came into effect this week. From July 1, most visa applications have increased by 25 per cent, with student visas (subclass 500) rising by $500 to $2500 and temporary graduate visas (subclass 485) jumping $1150 to $5750. Among the largest increases were to partner visas, which shot up to a whopping $11,710 — an increase of $2345 from $9365 — and the New Zealand family relationship visa, which almost doubled — up 198 per cent – from $445 to $1330. “I’ve never been so grateful for being on top of applying for my visa, because what do you mean it’s now $1000 as of today?” one working holiday-maker shared on TikTok. “Yesterday it was $670. That is wild.” Another TikToker called the New Zealand visa increase “crazy”. “I would have thought a couple hundred … I was just so surprised,” she said. “I feel so grateful that I got mine in when I did. I also feel so terrible for the people who haven’t got it in yet.” The increase to the temporary graduate visa fee comes just three months after it was doubled from $2300 to $4600. “TR fees increased again! Jesus, what an absolute jaffa,” one TikToker said. Former Immigration Department deputy secretary Dr Abul Rizvi said the fee increases were “really poor policy”. “They’re going to have to do something about net migration [to meet Anthony Albanese’s target], but this won’t get them there,” he said. “Australia’s visa fees were already amongst the highest in the world by a long way, particularly the student visa fee. “The UK student visa fee, for example, is about $1000, ours is now $2500. “The question is what is the government trying to achieve with such high fees, including for partners? “Why penalise Australians who have married foreigners with such a huge fee? What is the public policy objective? “I think it’s primarily a revenue-raising thing, they’re probably hoping it will bring down net overseas migration a bit but I don’t think it’ll do much. “If you think about partners, it’s probably not going to have much effect — if you’re a genuine partner, [the increased fee] is not going to mean you’re not going to get married. “It just means some people will have to scrimp and save a bit longer.” Dr Rizvi said the student visa fee increase would only have a “marginal” impact on bringing down numbers. “The bigger impact on student numbers is the refusal rate,” he said. It comes after Australia’s peak business body raised the alarm at the surprise visa fee hikes. Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar said on Thursday the increase far outpaced inflation and risked making Australia less attractive to skilled workers and international students. “Australia already had the most expensive student visa fees in the world,” he said in a statement. “Lifting that charge so dramatically in such a short period sends a poor signal to the global market.” Mr McKellar said higher visa costs would make Australia “a harder sell for visitors”, which could potentially impact tourism operators and educators. “Many businesses rely on skilled migrants, international students working in key sectors, and graduates who choose to stay and build their careers here,” he said. He added it was disappointing the government imposed these changes without consultation and without a public announcement. “Sneaking in major changes that carry drastic consequences is a poor way to treat the business community,” he said. Increases to various income thresholds for skilled migrants also came into effect on Wednesday. “Income thresholds are indexed annually so wages for skilled migrants increase at the same rate as Australian workers,” the Department of Home Affairs said in the announcement. “This ensures that people cannot use skilled migration to undercut Australian workers.” Mr McKellar said the visa increases come on top of other policy decisions making it harder for businesses to grow. “Visa charge hikes on top of a capital gains tax increase, new tax on trusts, minimum wage costs increasing beyond inflation, and employer incentives being cut — the government burdens are piling up,” he said. “The government cannot keep asking businesses to lift productivity while making it increasingly difficult to be productive.” It comes as Labor, the Coalition, and One Nation seek to assert their immigration credentials. Labor has dismissed criticism of booming immigration over its tenure as a result of Covid backlogs, while cracking down on character-related tests in the aftermath of the Bondi Beach terrorist attack. The Coalition, meanwhile, has sought to tie migration levels to housing completion, while One Nation has blamed immigration for the country’s housing and cost of living crisis. The latest figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) last month showed annual net overseas migration as of the December quarter 2025 was 300,960 people, down 9 per cent on the previous year. — with NewsWire

title: Bombshell new One Nation proposal - News.com.au
raw_text: One Nation unveils shock plan to reset net migration to zero One Nation has revealed a dramatic overhaul of Australia’s migration system, with hundreds of thousands fewer arrivals and a warning for those who don’t comply. EXCLUSIVE One Nation has unveiled a shock plan to “reset” Australia’s net overseas migration levels to zero by slashing the number of arrivals by more than 750,000 people. The major plan would take Australia’s current net overseas migration figure, which has a target of 225,000 in coming years, down to zero in a temporary measure lasting three years. It would then be reviewed and resettle at around 130,000 people a year. Labor’s current NOM target is 245,000 for 2026-27 and 225,000 for 2027-28. Want the latest political news? Download our new app so you never miss a headline. The temporary measures mirror radical reforms adopted in Canada that slowed a post-pandemic immigration surge by slashing overseas students and other arrivals. “Vested interests and elite economists will shriek at the prospect of these cuts,’’ Senator Hanson said. “But Canada has shown you can cut migrant numbers, take pressure off rents, and still grow the economy.” Plan to ‘restore living standards Senator Hanson said the plan would restore living standards, ease pressure on housing and essential services, and bring population growth back to a sustainable rate. “I know Australians are doing it tough. Families are competing with hundreds of people for rental accommodation,” she said. “Patients are stuck in ambulances because there are not enough hospital beds. Young Australians are being locked out of home ownership while wages and infrastructure fail to keep up. “Under Labor, the number of temporary visa holders has surged from 2 million in 2022 to roughly 3 million in 2026.” What is Net Overseas Migration? The net overseas migration figure is a poorly understood measure of the net gain or loss of population through immigration to and emigration from Australia. It is based on an international traveller’s duration of stay being in or out of Australia for 12 months or more over a 16-month period (the 12/16 month rule). It measures the difference between the number of incoming international travellers who stay in Australia for 12 months or more within 16 months and the number of outgoing international travellers. ‘Net negative’ migration reset One Nation’s plan aims to return the temporary migrant population to around 2017 levels and the international student population to 2015 levels. “Over the three years, net overseas migration will be net negative,” the One Nation policy document states. “Following this, One Nation’s net overseas migration ceiling of 130,000 per year would remain in place. “We will crack down on illegal migrant employment, cutting off illicit income and encouraging departures. Illegal migrants will be given three months to leave Australia. “Those who depart will be allowed to apply for a visa in the future. Those who remain unlawfully after this period will face immigration enforcement and a lifetime ban from re-entering Australia.” How the 750,000 reduction would work One Nation’s reduction in the temporary migrant population of approximately 750,000 would be achieved through restricting visa numbers and tightening eligibility criteria for temporary student and student graduate visas It aims to substantially restrict the ability of temporary students, graduates and skilled workers to sponsor family and dependants to Australia Crackdown on Overseas Students Under One Nation’s plan: -Overseas students must leave after completing their studies unless eligible for the targeted graduate pathway. -Graduate visa holders may move to an eligible employer-sponsored temporary skilled visa, but cannot obtain another graduate visa or switch back to a student visa from within Australia. -Temporary skilled workers may renew or replace their work visa if eligible, but cannot switch onshore into student, graduate, visitor or other temporary categories. -Visitors cannot apply for another visa from within Australia, apart from the specified exception for family-sponsored applications. Bridging visas would remain available for legitimate applications that are permitted to be made in Australia. Restricting onshore applications and visa switching aims to reduce the number of people entering and remaining in the bridging visa system. One Nation anticipates this will reduce the current bridging visa population from approximately 413,000 to 300,000 by year three. One Nation said universities would still be able to enrol more than 100,000 international students per year. “The temporary skilled migration program will remain available and be driven by employer demand,” the document states. “One Nation will maintain the existing seasonal worker programs, such as PALM and the working holiday maker program. “Employers will still be able to sponsor skilled migrants, but temporary skilled migration will no longer operate as a sham family migration pathway.” Divisions within One Nation One Nation has been criticised for its “incoherence” on migration policy after new MP David Farley suggested the party’s plan wasn’t that different to Labor’s policy. He argued the 130,000 NOM target excluded other forms of migration, including temporary workers from the Pacific Islands, skilled workers, and backpackers. The remarks sparked a rebuke from Senator Hanson. “The cuts will come from fewer international students and dependants, a dramatic reduction in temporary graduate visas and their dependants, and a much more targeted skilled migration program focused on the skills Australia genuinely needs,” she said. Opposition home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam said that One Nation was struggling to “get its story straight” on migration. “It is one thing to have a (NOM) number out there. It is another to go around and point at certain groups of visa classes and say we’ll reduce this,” Senator Duniam said.

title: ‘Tank the economy’: One Nation alert - News.com.au
raw_text: One Nation’s immigration plan will ‘tank economy’ to scale not seen since 1890s depression One Nation’s plan to slash immigration by 750,000 over three years would ‘tank the economy’, a prominent political commentator warns. One Nation’s plan to cut immigration by 750,000 over three years would “tank the Australian economy” on a scale not seen since the 1890s Depression, a prominent political commentator and author has warned. Speaking on ABC National Forum, George Megalogenis said the controversial policy would be disastrous, pointing out no government had ever purposefully caused a net outflow of migrants. Mr Megalogenis said One Nation was proposing to do something that had only happened four times in Australia’s history. Twice during the depressions of the 1890s and 1930s, and twice during the deployment of troops during the First and Second World Wars. “We’ve never had a period over the long run of our history where more people have left than have come the other way,” he said. “If you’re going to take 766,000 people out of the Australian economy and society for three years, you have tanked the Australian economy in a way that is on the scale of the depression of the 1890s and 1930s.” Net overseas migration has been falling from its post-COVID peak in 2023, when international borders reopened after the pandemic. Net overseas migration was 306,000 in 2024-25, down from 429,000 the previous year but still above the pre-COVID number of 241,000 in 2018-2019. One Nation’s plan would take Australia’s current net overseas migration figure down to zero for three years. It would then be reviewed and settled at around 130,000 people a year. Labor’s current target is 245,000 for 2026-27 and 225,000 for 2027-28. One Nation will follow ‘will of the people’, Joyce says One Nation treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce appeared alongside Multicultural Affairs Minister Anne Aly and opposition frontbencher Andrew Hastie on ABC’s National Forum on migration. Mr Joyce defended One Nation’s proposal, saying the party’s policy would focus immediately on the 3 million temporary visa holders as a way to drastically reduce net migration. “We’ve said quite clearly that you can’t have 3 million temporary visa holders walking around Australia; that means it’s going from a country to a caravan park,” Mr Joyce said. Mr Joyce was pressed by host David Speers on how much the proposal would cost in jobs, income and the budget. “The issue of what it is going to cost I think is contentious, but I have no concern about following the will of the Australian people,” Mr Joyce said. “I think the Australian people are sort of tired of the fact that you have to go to an economist to come up with public policy, to go to the Parliamentary Budget Office, and, to be quite frank, I have been around this game for a while and I have never seen a forward estimates in any budgetary paper be even close to the mark. “The will of the Australian people is so pronounced, this has to be dealt with, we will deal with it.” Mr Joyce said he wasn’t worried about what the Parliamentary Budget Office or another office might conclude about the policy, saying “they’re not elected, I am.” Ms Aly agreed migration numbers had been too high, particularly post-Covid, but said the challenge was how to bring those numbers down in a manageable way. “The difficulty is doing it in a way that preserves the integrity of the migration system, but that creates a system that is fair for everybody and one that responds to the needs of Australia and in the national interest of Australia,” she said. Mr Hastie said the Coalition was committed to tying net overseas migration to the number of homes being built each year. “Last year we built 170,000 homes and the net overseas migration figures for the last four years have been well above that and we’re now seeing the consequences of that with Australians not being able to find homes,” he said. “I’ve seen people waking up in their cars down on the beach in Western Australia. I know of children who are living in tents and caravans because our housing stock has not kept pace with the growth of immigration.” ‘Kill the economy’ Since the announcement on Monday, One Nation’s plan has been slammed by the government, opposition, farmers and business groups. Environment Minister Murray Watt said the plan would “kill the Australian economy and kill regional economies in particular”, pointing to early industry responses including farmers. “I mean, I don’t know when the last time Barnaby Joyce or Pauline Hanson walked into a doctor’s clinic, a hospital, an aged-care facility, to a construction site, to a country pub, to see the number of migrants who are working in these populations,” he said. Senator Watt said Labor understood “that we do need to bring down the number of migrants coming into Australia”, and that the Albanese government had been “doing that since we came to office and we intend to do more”. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the policy raised more questions than it answered. More Coverage “I am deeply concerned about what it means for individual farmers, for individual businesses, for builders, for pub owners, for cafe owners,” he said on Monday. The National Farmers Federation said the plan would hurt regional Australia, where temporary workers “help put food on tables, with backpackers alone filling roughly one in seven farm jobs nationally”. The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry also warned “major cuts that reduce skilled migration” would put the economy at risk.

When Prime Minister Anthony Albanese likened Narendra Modi to Bruce Springsteen in 2023, it captured more than the spectacle surrounding the Indian leader's visit. Addressing a lively crowd at Sydney's Qudos Bank Arena, Albanese remarked that the rock legend was the last person he'd seen on stage there, adding that "he didn't get the welcome that Prime Minister Modi has got". It reflected the cordiality between the two leaders, who have helped transform a relationship once seen as rich in untapped potential into what both now describe as a "comprehensive strategic partnership". But Albanese's comments also drew sharp criticism from some parts of the Indian diaspora and human rights advocates, who argued that the glowing reception glossed over allegations of human rights abuses under Modi's leadership — claims he has strenuously denied. The response captured the stark divide in public opinion about Modi, who is widely celebrated by supporters for driving economic growth and India's global profile, but whose leadership is also the subject of sustained international scrutiny from human rights organisations and democracy monitors. Now, as the Indian prime minister returns to Australia for his third visit in nearly 12 years, the setting has shifted to Melbourne, where another large diaspora gathering is expected to showcase the public enthusiasm that has become a defining feature of his overseas outreach. Beyond the flags, crowds and political theatre, the visit comes at a more complex moment for the relationship between the two nations. Experts say it will test whether Albanese and Modi's close relationship can translate into concrete outcomes as both navigate a changing regional environment, domestic pressures and more difficult conversations around visa policies and migration, trade, and differing approaches to global issues, including sanctions against Russia and Iran. The visit also offers an opportunity to examine a relationship that has become one of Australia's most important in the Indo-Pacific — shaped by geopolitics, economic ambition and the realities of a growing diaspora, including the opportunities and challenges that come with closer ties. From distance to strategic alignment The friendly diplomacy between Albanese and Modi contrasts with earlier periods in Australia-India relations. Although diplomatic ties with Australia were established before India's independence in 1947, the two countries spent decades navigating differences over the Cold War, nuclear policy, migration and Australia's engagement with Asia. The legacy of the White Australia Policy and disagreements among earlier leaders also affected bilateral ties at various points. Modi's 2014 visit, the first by an Indian prime minister to Australia in more than three decades, marked a turning point in resetting ties beyond the familiar territory of cricket and community links. Since then, cooperation has expanded through trade, the Quad — the strategic grouping of Australia, India, Japan and the United States — alongside defence engagement, critical minerals and supply chain partnerships, with both countries seeing each other as important partners in a more contested Indo-Pacific. Teesta Prakash, a research fellow in security and geopolitics at the Australia India Institute, says Modi's repeated visits reflect how significantly Australia's role has grown in India's strategic thinking. "This is the most amount of times any Indian prime minister has visited Australia, which underscores just how important Australia is to India's strategic imagination," she tells SBS News. Prakash says Modi's first visit was largely about resetting the relationship after he came to office. Twelve years on, with the broader strategic framework now established, the focus has shifted towards implementation. "So this trip is less likely to focus on announcing new strategic frameworks, but more on delivering concrete outcomes, in defence, defence industry, critical minerals — uranium included —technology partnerships and supply chain resilience." What to expect from Modi's visit With Modi scheduled to be in Melbourne on Wednesday evening, his third visit is expected to focus on delivery. Pradeep Taneja, a senior lecturer in Asian politics at the University of Melbourne, says Australia has described India as a "top-tier" security partner and expects the visit to build on existing areas of collaboration. "In terms of concrete outcomes, it is possible that some agreements may be signed that build on the ongoing collaboration in critical minerals and energy security," he tells SBS News. But I don't expect any big bang announcements during this visit. Economic ties are also expected to feature prominently. The Australia-India Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement, which came into force in late 2022, substantially lowered tariffs and expanded market access across a wide range of goods and services, opening Australia's market to Indian exports while giving Australian businesses improved access to India. Negotiations are continuing on a broader Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement, which aims to deepen the economic partnership. Agriculture, however, remains one of the more sensitive issues. Australia has long sought greater access to India's agricultural market, while India's government has resisted opening sectors such as dairy, wheat, rice and sugar, arguing they are critical to the livelihoods of millions of small farmers. The differing scales and structures of the farming sector across the two countries mean agriculture is expected to remain one of the more challenging areas in negotiations towards a comprehensive trade deal. Defence will be another key area to watch. Cooperation has expanded through military exercises, maritime engagement and deeper coordination in the Indo-Pacific, with both countries seeking to move from strategic alignment towards practical collaboration. Lisa Singh, CEO of the Australia India Institute at the University of Melbourne, says the visit will ultimately be judged by whether commitments translate into action. These prime ministerial visits are such a significant moment to move the relationship forward. "New commitments in defence are one important area that both nations can show they are doing that, highlighting that our trusted partnership is not just words but actions that will help make our nations and region safer," Singh said in a statement to SBS News. What's driving the partnership The transformation in India-Australia ties reflects a broader shift in the Indo-Pacific. China's growing military and economic influence has heightened strategic competition across the region, and concerns over supply chain resilience have pushed Canberra and New Delhi into closer alignment. Through the Quad and other bilateral initiatives, the two countries have expanded cooperation on defence, maritime security, critical minerals, clean energy and technology as they seek to strengthen regional stability and reduce dependence on any single partner. Albanese has also framed the relationship through the lens of India's growing economic weight. In an address to the parliament in May, he described India as "a global economic powerhouse" and said it was on track to become the world's third-largest economy this decade, calling it "an extraordinary opportunity for us in our region". Taneja says uncertainty over the future strategic role of the US has prompted Australia to diversify its strategic partnerships. "India is now seen as an important partner because the interests of the two countries align more closely than they did in the past," he says. Taneja says while both governments frequently speak of shared democratic values and a free and open Indo-Pacific, the relationship is ultimately shaped by strategic interests. "Despite claims of shared values, the fact remains that the relations between Australia and India are based on shared interests." Shared values play a secondary role in bilateral relations. The Modi factor: diaspora and diplomacy Beyond official meetings, Modi is expected to prioritise engagement with the Indian diaspora — a common feature of his international visits. Since becoming prime minister in 2014, he has held numerous large-scale diaspora events around the world. His decision to address supporters in Melbourne — rather than Sydney, as he did in 2023 — reflects the changing geography of Australia's Indian community, with Victoria home to one of the country's largest Indian-born populations. The visit also comes as Melbourne debates the proposed 'Little India' cultural precinct in Docklands on the western end of the CBD, which supporters say would recognise the Indian community's contribution to the city. Nationally, the timing is significant. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, people born in India are now Australia's largest overseas-born population for the first time on record, narrowly overtaking those born in England. But the relationship between diaspora and diplomacy is unfolding alongside a more contested migration debate in Australia. The Albanese government has tightened student visa settings and sought to reduce net overseas migration, while visa scrutiny has intensified and anti-immigration rhetoric has become more prominent in domestic politics. Prakash says while migration is ultimately a sovereign policy decision, it is one of the issues Modi could raise with Albanese, much like he raised concerns over the vandalism of Hindu temples during his 2023 visit. "Migration specifically is a sovereign domestic decision, and while obviously it impacts Indian potential students or migrants who were looking to move to Australia. I think there's a solid understanding that each country makes decisions on this specific front on its own comparative advantages and priorities," she says. "So, I don't think it risks broader relationships, but it does ask the leaders to have uncomfortable conversations." Like previous visits, Modi's arrival is also expected to attract both supporters and protesters. Demonstrations during his 2023 visit highlighted the political diversity of Australia's Indian diaspora, with at times polarised views on the Modi government's domestic policies and wider political debates unfolding in India.
