One of the most enduring points of contention remains the 2002 riots in Gujarat, in western India, which occurred while Modi was chief minister of the state. Official figures state more than 1,000 people — the majority of them Muslim and more than 250 Hindus — were murdered in a three-month outbreak of violence, sparked by a train fire that killed 59 Hindu pilgrims. Modi faced accusations over his handling of the violence but was later cleared of personal wrongdoing by Indian investigative bodies and the courts. Critics continue to cite the riots as emblematic of broader concerns about accountability and minority rights in the Hindu-majority country, while supporters argue the matter has been thoroughly examined and legally resolved. Those debates resurfaced internationally following the 2023 BBC documentary, India: The Modi Question, which examined the Gujarat violence and its political aftermath. The documentary was banned in India, while the Indian government dismissed it as biased and rejected its conclusions. The BBC said the documentary was "rigorously researched" and featured a range of opinions and experts. The broadcaster said in a statement that it had given the Indian government a right of reply, but the government had declined to respond. India has also fallen sharply in global press freedom rankings, with Reporters Without Borders placing it at 157 out of 180 countries, citing increasing risks to journalists and concerns about political pressure on media independence. Modi's own engagement with the media has also drawn scrutiny. Since becoming the prime minister in 2014, he has not held a traditional solo press conference and has rarely taken unscripted questions from journalists during his foreign jaunts. Human Rights Watch's (HRW) latest report on India states the country's "slide to authoritarianism under the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party-led government continued [in 2025], with increased vilification of Muslims and government critics". The BJP's performance in India's 2024 general election also changed the political landscape, with Modi losing his outright majority and returning to power as the head of a coalition government after the party lost 63 seats compared with the previous election. Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at HRW, says these concerns are not confined to India's borders, with political tensions also being felt within parts of the diaspora. I think it is important to see that there is a growing sort of muscular nationalism and politics of hate [in India]. "That is also being exported among the diaspora. So even the communities that lived in far greater harmony before are feeling those tensions when they're living abroad because of what is happening in India," she tells SBS News. Following Modi's 2023 visit, Albanese dismissed suggestions he had shared a stage with a "tyrant", saying India was "a great democracy". The push for strategic cooperation These debates are happening at the same time as a broader foreign policy conversation is unfolding. India's strategic autonomy continues to shape its international relationships, including its ties with Russia and Iran. India has maintained defence and energy links with Russia and has not joined with Australia and other Western nations in imposing sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The government has also maintained its relationship with Iran despite documented evidence of severe human rights violations under the Iranian regime, citing its importance for India's energy, connectivity and regional interests. India is also part of BRICS, a group that includes countries like Russia and China, reflecting its non-aligned approach to global politics. For Australia, these uncomfortable differences exist alongside a growing push towards strategic cooperation. When asked about India's relationship with Russia ahead of Modi's 2023 visit, Albanese acknowledged the different histories shaping the two countries' foreign policies. "We have very different histories, of course ... India has been a leader of the Non-Aligned Movement for such a long period of time," he said at the time, referencing the group of more than 120 countries that are not formally aligned with or against any major international power bloc. A partnership entering a new phase Returning to the moment Albanese welcomed Modi on stage in 2023 stirs mixed feelings for some. "Prime Minister Modi is 'the boss'," he declared, referencing the colloquial nickname for US rock legend Springsteen. However, for many in the Indian diaspora, who may not be Springsteen fans, it likely resonated differently — reflecting the power wielded by a leader who has become central to India's global image. Beyond the symbolism, the Australia-India partnership is stronger than it was a decade ago — and far more complex. It now involves defence cooperation, supply chains, migration, education, diaspora politics and a growing debate about how democracies engage with each other in a more uncertain world. Singh says the next phase will depend on whether both countries can turn alignment into lasting cooperation. The question now is how both nations navigate their future partnership amidst the current backdrop of global uncertainty. "I hope new investment opportunities are created and that we work further on building trusted supply chains in goods and technology that will overcome the shocks of the future," she says. As Modi arrives in Melbourne, the scale of the community event will once again highlight the strength of the people-to-people connection. But the future of the relationship will be defined by what happens after the applause fades. The challenge for both countries is whether they can continue expanding a partnership that has become strategically important while managing the tensions that come with being closer than ever. title: Is Hanson’s rise Albanese’s fall? Not so fast - SMH.com.au
raw_text: A month ago, Anthony Albanese gave a remarkably sanguine admission of the fact that sometimes there is nothing you can do to stop political decline. “I firmly believe that if you govern in the right way, and you get the policies right, then the politics will look after itself,” he told The Saturday Paper. “And if it doesn’t, due to circumstances beyond your control, well, that’s OK.” Is Labor in political decline? The opinion of pundits right now seems drastically split. On one hand, there is acceptance that Labor is very likely to win the next federal election – because it starts with a huge seat majority and the conservative vote is split between teals, One Nation and the Coalition. At the same time, there is a growing hum of commentary suggesting the government is in trouble, Albanese is unpopular and fighting back could be tough. Saturday’s result in the byelection for the West Australian state seat of Secret Harbour will amplify that hum. The WA Labor government suffered a huge swing against it, its MP’s primary vote being almost halved. One Nation won decisively. Albanese would have had a good sense this was coming: context for the fact that last week, visiting the state, he gave a clear indication he is aware that anything might happen between now and the next federal election. That indication came in the form of a clear commitment to continue the ridiculously generous deal WA gets on the GST. This undermines his first point from last month – that if policies are right, the politics will look after themselves. The WA GST deal is bad policy, hugely expensive and unfair to all other states and the people who live in them – as the Productivity Commission’s recent interim report made clear. But the commitment shows Albanese is entirely genuine when he refers to the possibility of circumstances running beyond you. The only good reason to keep the GST deal is the knowledge that the moment Labor breaks its word, every one of its opponents in WA will move in for the kill. And the only reason that matters is if you believe it is possible that, at the 2028 election, those WA seats might turn out to be essential. Albanese is not betting Labor will be in political strife by 2028, but he is obviously taking out insurance just in case. On the politics, this is understandable. title: ‘Could see myself sitting here’: One Nation MP Farley gatecrashes Liberal meeting - SMH.com.au
raw_text: One Nation MP David Farley has fuelled speculation about his future in Pauline Hanson’s party after accidentally walking into a private meeting of more than 20 Liberal MPs – then telling them he could see himself sitting with them. The extraordinary encounter happened in Parliament House last Wednesday when Farley wandered into a regular meeting of Liberal MPs from marginal seats. Several Liberals present said the Farrer MP took a while to realise he was in the wrong room before turning to leave. “I could see myself sitting here,” Farley told the MPs, before walking out. “We were all taken aback, to be honest,” one Liberal MP said. “It was a very loose thing to say.” Farley confirmed the incident on Monday, but portrayed it as an off-the-cuff joke after accidentally entering the room. He said the Liberal MPs had a “who-hit-John” look on their faces, silent with their mouths open, before he “filled the empty space with my quip” and left. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said Farley was currently a member of One Nation “but certainly let’s see what the future holds”. “He’s a decent fellow, I’ve met him a couple of times,” Hastie told ABC’s 7.30. The remark comes at an awkward time for One Nation, with Farley again publicly at odds with Hanson over one of the party’s central political issues. The Farrer MP told ABC’s Insiders that while One Nation wanted to reduce net overseas migration to 130,000, it would allow another 100,000 migrant workers through skilled visas, backpacker programs and the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. That would put the effective number at about 230,000 – broadly in line with Labor’s forecast of 225,000 by 2027–28. Hanson moved quickly to reject Farley’s interpretation, insisting One Nation’s policy was to cut net overseas migration to 130,000, with some short-term agricultural workers excluded from the official measure. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce was then sent out to clean up the mess, telling Sunrise that Farley had simply got it wrong. “Show me a political career where people haven’t made a mistake, and I’ll show you a person who’s not told the truth.” Joyce said One Nation had seemingly raised the matter with Farley but refused to elaborate. “Oh, look, I’m not going to throw anybody under a bus,” he said. “When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect, and that’s what happens. God knows I’ve done it enough.” “I think [Farley] would have been offended by [One Nation’s head of operations] James Ashby going on News24 last night with a mop and essentially mocking what I thought were his thoughtful contributions on [ABC’s] Insiders yesterday,” Hastie said. Hastie was referring to Ashby’s appearance on News24 on Sunday night where he brandished a mop and clarified One Nation’s migration policies, stating he’d spoken to Farley and that “people make mistakes”. “For a new member of parliament, it’s always difficult getting your head around those [net overseas migration] numbers,” Ashby said. Farley’s comments were also savaged by online news site One News Australia, which branded his appearance a “rookie blunder” and claimed his “clueless” performance had given Labor an “escape route” from its migration policy. The criticism is notable given One News Australia’s origins as the One Nation Supporters Network before it was rebranded as a news organisation. The site and the party say they have no affiliation, although its coverage is strongly pro-One Nation and Hanson. Farley was previously counselled by Hanson during the Farrer byelection campaign after he agreed a net migration figure of 306,000 last year was “probably not” too many. The pair also exchanged harsh words after it was revealed that he’d previously tried to seek preselection with Labor for the seat and not informed anyone within One Nation before it was revealed by this masthead. Farley has already shown he is prepared to depart from Hanson’s position in the parliament. Last week he voted with the Coalition on an amendment to Labor’s wagering legislation, despite Hanson having previously committed to supporting the government’s ban on foreign matched lotteries. His growing independence is being watched closely by Coalition MPs, particularly given his conservative and agricultural background. Sources in the Coalition said Opposition Leader Angus Taylor knew Farley from his time as an agribusiness leader and could potentially use the relationship to court him in future, although there are no immediate plans to do so. “He is a Nat or a country Liberal, not a populist,” one Liberal MP said. Farley told Insiders he came from the conservative LNP tradition, joined the Nationals after returning to Farrer and later explored joining Labor and running as an independent. He ultimately chose One Nation because he said it offered the “political courage” and “tenacity” he wanted. “I have the full support of the party to pursue what I’m doing, especially for Farrer,” he said. title: Labor quietly pauses working holidaymaker visas as stoush over backpackers brews - SMH.com.au
raw_text: The Albanese government has quietly paused working holidaymaker visa applications from 24 countries as it seeks to wrest control of the migration system while a political stoush brews over whether to curtail the number of backpackers who come to Australia. Migration and travel agents have told the tourism industry they have been detecting delays in processing times for countries with uncapped backpacker places since the beginning of July, while the pause on applications from countries with caps was introduced without notice in the last month. Backpacker and Youth Tourism Advisory Panel chair Peta Zietsch said this would have a knock-on effect for tourism operators and regional employers who relied on backpackers for seasonal work, and who would usually expect young Europeans to arrive in Australia soon for the summer period. Zietsch said it also risked deterring backpackers when combined with the recent rise in visa fees, which increased from $670 to $840 for first visas and $1000 for second- and third-year visas last month. “Rather than placing barriers in the way of the working holidaymaker program, we should be looking at ways to attract more young international travellers here,” she said. Working holidaymakers, who have surged in number since the pandemic, were drawn into the political debate over immigration this week as both Labor and the Coalition fine-tune their plans for lowering Australia’s migrant intake. Labor’s May budget papers had already flagged that the government wanted to expand the use of ballots, or lotteries, to deal with demand for the popular visas and to better control numbers. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke was expected to use his delayed National Press Club address to outline how this would inform his plan to meet a 225,000 net migration target within two years. targeted to reduce overall migration to about 180,000, during a wide-ranging speech on Wednesday that raised eyebrows among his colleagues. But Nationals leader Matt Canavan quickly knocked back the idea, saying on Friday: “They’re just not the problem, so that won’t be targeted.” Canavan told Radio National: “It’s not been the cause of the migration crisis we’re seeing in Australia since the end of COVID. So, what we clearly need to do is look at those programs that have blown out and are causing so much stress on the infrastructure and services and housing of this country.” Data, however, shows that working holidaymakers have been a key driver of higher migration since 2022. They made up 17.5 per cent of the net migration figure in 2024-25. This masthead reported in 2024 and 2025 that working backpacker numbers had reached new highs, driven by Morrison government changes that expanded eligibility for workers, particularly British nationals who no longer had to complete regional work to stay longer in the country. Latest government data from June 30 shows this trend has continued: there were 225,648 working holidaymakers in the country at the end of the financial year, which is the highest June data on record. It compares with 210,971 in June 2025, and 173,216 in June 2024 – all of which were also June records at the time. There are two working holidaymaker visas. The first visa stream is uncapped and has 19 partner countries, including the United Kingdom, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan – meaning places are demand-driven. The second visa stream is capped. It applies to a further 29 countries, which are allocated between 100 and 5000 places a year. They include Argentina, Indonesia, Austria and Israel. Three of the countries in the capped category – China, India and Vietnam – have a lottery system regulating who can apply at what time of year. The remaining countries have all been put on pause, except for Turkey and San Marino, which have just 100 places each. The Department of Home Affairs website says applications could be paused when the cap is nearly filled, or to spread applications throughout the year. “Lodgements may also be paused to support the government’s migration settings while ensuring the program operates sustainably,” it says. The department did not respond to questions about why the majority of applications had been paused, given the annual caps reset just six weeks ago. Immigration expert Abul Rizvi said pausing so many countries at once was highly unusual. “Where we are with working holidaymaker numbers now is higher than anything before COVID by a long way,” he said. “I suspect it’s a temporary pause to work out how to manage the demand, or to organise the lottery for other countries.” The government has indicated it could expand the lottery system to other countries to manage arrivals. And while the first year visa is capped, the second and third years are not. Capping those visas, or removing the third-year visa that was introduced during the pandemic, would be another option for the government to reduce net migration by making more people leave the country earlier. Rizvi said removing the third visa could bring down net migration by between 5000 and 10,000 people in a full year. “It would get Matt Canavan and Pauline Hanson cross, as well as farmers and regional tourism businesses,” he said. The contest over working holidaymaker visas demonstrates the challenges for the Coalition as it seeks to drive down migrant numbers without affecting regional areas that rely on labour migration. One Nation would also hit a snag in its efforts to retain working holidaymaker visas for regional workforces while at the same time promising to only issue 130,000 visas a year across the entire migration system. title: Pub test: Albanese faces dire warnings that migration plan risks shuttering hotels - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is facing blowback from industry groups over his migration overhaul amid fears that regional pubs will shut down and food security will be compromised without enough foreign workers. As Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke scrambles to work out how to rein in migration without damaging the economy, junior international education minister Julian Hill has used new powers to kill a dodgy graduate diploma course being used by tens of thousands of international students to visa-hop and extend their stay by years. Labor is aiming to bring net overseas migration from 300,000 down to its target of 225,000 after years of missed forecasts. A suite of changes to tighten up the system was abruptly delayed last month after ministers said the policy needed more work. One Nation and the Coalition are proposing large cuts to the inflow of migrants as fresh national accounts show the economy struggling to keep up with population growth. Separate to measures likely to be announced in coming weeks, this masthead revealed last month that Labor had quietly paused working holidaymaker visa applications from 24 countries. Two dozen peak bodies wrote to Albanese on Wednesday about those changes, which they said could hurt industries and test Australia’s arrangement with Asian nations to provide fertiliser in return for food. Backpackers make up around 44 per cent of the horticultural peak harvest workforce. “We are collectively calling for immediate clarity on your government’s intent concerning proposed reform of the [working holidaymaker] program, the extent and effect of current administrative actions, and a commitment to consult,” the industry chiefs said. Groups including the National Farmers Federation, Council of Small Businesses of Australia, Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association, and a range of agricultural groups said the backpacker scheme performed a dual role. As tourists, they argued, working holidaymakers spent more time in regional areas than other visitors. As workers, the letter said, “restaurants, cafes, hotels, pubs, catering operators, retail and the care sectors, including childcare and early learning, rely on [backpackers]”. “These are precisely the services that make a regional community liveable,” they said. The business groups’ decision to unite against changes to backpacker visas reflects the economic trade-offs involved in the migration debate. This masthead previously reported that ministers were concerned about the effect of proposed changes on the budget bottom line and labour shortages in critical industries. Australian Hotels Association chief executive Stephen Ferguson said pubs and clubs relied on backpackers and international students because the system for training locals was broken. He criticised the government for de-prioritising hospitality training even though the sector contributed $74 million to the Skilling Australians Fund. “If they helped us train our own, we’d be far less reliant on immigration at least as it relates to the kitchen, which is our chronic problem,” he said, noting it took nine months to a year to bring a worker into the country after their application was approved. Cathal Leslie, a former economist at the Productivity Commission, rubbished the concerns of big business on Thursday, writing that Australia could drop the ATAR score required to study to be a doctor, increase wages for aged care nursing to attract locals and stop using cheap labour instead of innovating. “Our lacklustre productivity performance has coincided with a migration program that is less skilled than advertised,” he said in the Australian Financial Review, arguing for net negative migration. Backpackers have proved a divisive issue. Both the Nationals and One Nation have pledged to protect the streams of visitors into regional areas. There is bipartisan support for moves to reduce the number of international students. title: ‘One of the great Australian achievements’: Howard praises immigration - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Former prime minister John Howard says immigration has been one of Australia’s great success stories and that the best way for politicians to deal with the rise of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson is to not pay her too much attention. In a call for calm after months of increasing hostility over Australia’s immigration intake, driven by One Nation’s surge to a historic high, Howard said everybody, irrespective of their ethnic background, should feel they are a part of Australia. “We wanted migrants who would embrace this country. We didn’t require of them that they forget the country of their birth. Nobody wants you to do that,” he said. “If your parents were born in Italy, or if they were born in Lebanon, if they were born in China, why should you ask of them that they give up affection for the country of their ancestry? We did require of them that they become fully part of the Australian community.” Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on Thursday announced a series of measures aimed at curbing temporary migration, including limits on partner visas for students, and a backpacker ballot. The measures have been broadly accepted by the university sector and they have drawn condemnation from farmers alarmed about workforce shortages to pick crops, highlighting the challenges of making even small changes to the immigration intake without a backlash from a range of lobby groups. Burke said Australia was facing a much broader challenge over the structure of its immigration program, which has become reliant on temporary migration and is at risk of creating a guest worker economy. “This is one of the things I’m very worried about,” Burke said in an interview. “I don’t have an immediate fix to it.” The temporary migrant workforce now accounts for more than 16 per cent of the working-age population, filling offices, farms and restaurants across the country without the rights of permanent residents or citizens. The government does not have the legislative tools to address the demand-driven system without support from the Coalition. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has echoed Hanson’s claims that Australia has a problem with “mass migration” and he rejected Labor’s attempts to legislate new powers to tackle the demand-driven system without a “serious cut to the numbers and a serious improvement in the standards”. Howard’s 2001 slogan, “We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come”, came to define decades of refugee politics. But his government also turbocharged the demand-driven temporary migration system by handing control over temporary migration to business, allowing employers and universities to sponsor staff and students with minimal government oversight. The policies under the old 457 visa were designed to fill labour shortages, reduce taxpayer funding for universities and drive economic growth. They also created the foundation for the current explosion in temporary migration. More than 1 million temporary migrant visas were issued last year, based on business and education demand, not government regulation. “It’s important to have a migration program that caters for reasonable expectations of a number of things, including shortages of skilled migrants,” Howard said. Australia’s second longest serving prime minister would not comment on the long-term implications of his government’s temporary migration policies. “The Labor Party is obviously the government now, and there’s always more pressure for the government party, but it’s a community issue and I want Australia to be a happy family.” One Nation is polling well above the Coalition and just one percentage point lower than Labor on first preference votes, according to the latest Resolve Political Monitor. Howard was the Liberal leader when Hanson was first pre-selected as a Liberal candidate in 1996, before she was disendorsed after offensive comments against Indigenous Australians. Hanson, at age 41, entered parliament as an independent, beginning an almost three-decade career in politics based largely on anti-immigration policies that have now resulted in her party eclipsing the Coalition as the dominant challenger to the Labor government. “What I said was that we shouldn’t pay too much attention to her and I think that was a sensible approach then,” Howard said. Howard said Australia had become more divided. “It only, in my view, started to go off the rails when we started talking in tribes,” he said. “What I know is that the policy we followed for decades worked. It’s been one of the great Australian achievements that we’ve taken people from all around the world.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: Police injured as protesters descend on homes for asylum seekers in England - The Age
raw_text: Thetford: Angry residents have turned on police in a clash over asylum seekers in an English town where homes have been used to house migrants, with some protesters trying to break into a property to force the new arrivals to leave. A crowd of about 100 residents gathered in the Norfolk town of Thetford over two nights to try to stop local homes from being used to offer emergency accommodation for asylum seekers, including many who cross the English Channel by boat. Authorities had to evacuate at least five of the migrants when the protest turned violent on Wednesday night, the second night of the protests, as residents threw eggs and rocks at the house as well as the police. The town was calmer on Thursday night (early on Friday, AEST) after police applied public safety powers to require people to remove balaclavas and other face coverings or risk being arrested. While dozens of people gathered on the third night of protests, police issued 10 dispersal notices to prevent any violence. The unrest is the latest example of violence over migration after years of growing anger at the arrival of thousands of asylum seekers, many of whom are housed in hotels or homes in residential areas. Around 36,000 people arrived by small boat over the year to the end of May, straining the government’s capacity to house them despite plans to turn former military bases into asylum seeker camps. Tempers in Thetford, halfway between Cambridge and Norwich, were already raw over government plans to house about 1000 migrants at an air base south of the town. Opponents are planning a public rally against the plan later this month. The angry scenes over the past few nights included men in black balaclavas confronting police in the apparent belief that authorities were protecting the asylum seekers rather than the community. While the gatherings were largely peaceful on Tuesday night, they turned violent on Wednesday night when police stopped protesters trying to break into the ground floor of a home with asylum seekers living upstairs. “As police intervened, members of the group became physically aggressive towards officers,” Norfolk Police said. “Two were taken to hospital after a male officer was struck with a rock and a female officer was seriously bitten, breaking the skin. A third officer was also spat at.” Police said one man, 68, a resident of Thetford, was charged with possession of an offensive weapon – a wooden bat – on Wednesday night. He was released on bail and is due to appear in court on August 25. Another man, aged in his 30s, was arrested after the first night of unrest on suspicion of a public order offence, but was released and issued with a conditional caution. Two men, both in their 40s, were arrested on the third night of the protests. One was detained on suspicion of inciting racial hatred the previous evening. The second was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly. Assistant Chief Constable Julie Dean said the police supported the right to peaceful protest but would act against violence, intimidation or criminal behaviour. “Our role is to keep people safe. We have a duty to protect everyone in our communities, maintain public order and prevent harm,” she said on Thursday afternoon, local time (about 10.30pm AEST). “We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties.” One protester drew a direct link with recent violence in Belfast, where local residents burned homes being used to house asylum seekers, according to the Eastern Daily Press. “They got them out, kicked them out, and the ones that didn’t go, they burned the house down,” the woman told the local newspaper. “I’m not saying that we would do it, I’m not an arsonist. “At the end of the day, we got them removed.” A video shared on TikTok showed dozens of police escorting a small group of asylum seekers while protesters jeered, with some yelling: “Get them out.” Reform UK councillor Scott Hussey, a cabinet member at Norfolk County Council, highlighted the scale of the police response in a post on X that said “half of Norfolk police” were guarding the house with migrants. A key issue in public debate is how a residential property can be converted into a “house of multiple occupancy” (HMO), in which each room can be rented under a separate tenancy. Companies including Serco have used HMO properties to provide housing services to the Home Office to help with the arrival of asylum seekers, but this is controversial in residential areas where local people oppose the new arrivals. The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, condemned the violence and said some local residents told him they feared for their safety. Jermy, a former mayor of Thetford, said he opposed the plan to turn the air force base at nearby Barnham into a camp for asylum seekers. About 193,000 people crossed in small boats to reach the UK over the seven years to 2025, according to the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford. Citizens of six countries – Iran, Afghanistan, Iraq, Albania, Syria and Eritrea – made up 65 per cent of those crossing. Asylum was granted to 62 per cent of all those who came by small boat. “Around 36,000 people arrived by small boat in the year ending 31 May 2026, 13 per cent less than in the same period the year before,” it said. The fall in arrivals has been much steeper over the first five months of this calendar year. Only 9000 crossed in that period, down 38 per cent on the same period last year. title: ‘Total disregard’: Top officials warned Labor of NZ rules before Kiwi migrants surged - The Age
raw_text: The Albanese government overlooked internal warnings there would be an influx of New Zealanders under plans to give them easier access to welfare and citizenship, which has turned into one of Labor’s thorniest challenges in driving down the migration rate. The burst in Kiwis coming to Australia has been one of the biggest blowouts in the net overseas migration rate since the pandemic, a prospect that was raised by top officials at the time Prime Minister Anthony Albanese made the key policy move early in his first term. Sources familiar with cabinet deliberations at the time, not permitted to speak in public, said officials from Treasury and Home Affairs expressed serious concerns that the move would create too big an incentive for Kiwis to move to Australia, particularly if Australia had a healthier job market and economy. New Zealand subsequently went into recession, sparking more movement. The net intake of New Zealanders surged to 38,000 per year in the two years after Albanese widened benefits and citizenship pathways in July 2023 – compared to about 8000 or fewer before the pandemic. Consistent demand and uncapped places meant New Zealanders on special visas made up 12.5 per cent of the net migration figure in the 2024-25 financial year. Labor is now scrambling to find ways to reduce net migration after consistently overshooting its targets, while the Coalition and One Nation have tied themselves in knots advocating for more drastic cuts. As migration and its interplay with the cost of living rise to the top of the political agenda, this masthead revealed in recent days that the government is mulling increasing deportations for visa overstayers. It also quietly paused backpacker visas from 24 countries. Treasurer Jim Chalmers warned about the costs of lowering migration on Monday, arguing the Coalition was intent on “dividing the country” and crashing the economy. The New Zealand surge coincided with Albanese’s decision in 2023 to reverse a Howard-era policy by allowing New Zealanders to gain citizenship after four years without becoming permanent residents first. It also gave New Zealanders quicker access to Medicare and the family tax benefit once they arrived. Albanese said at the time that the Howard-era changes had made citizenship harder for Kiwis and that the 2023 change harmonised rules between the nations. But department officials feared that even if the economies were about as healthy as each other, the relaxed rules would still create a large incentive for New Zealanders because Australia is a bigger and wealthier country. Labor warmed relations with Jacinda Ardern’s government after the progressive leader sparred with Scott Morrison over deportations of criminal dual citizens. The Albanese government policy to grant access to Medicare stopped short of offering the same access to the NDIS and other welfare items. Migration expert and former department official Abul Rizvi said the 2023 policy change was “made with total disregard to the impact on [net overseas migration].” Asked about the bureaucratic alarm bells, a spokesman for Burke said Labor reversed the Howard-era rules because the old settings created “intolerable circumstance where young people would spend their whole life in Australia only to reach uni and discover they were ineligible for HECS.” Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows around 30,000 New Zealanders were arriving each year before the pandemic, while between 22,000 and 27,000 left. This meant their overall impact on the net migration figure was small – between 2.5 per cent and 3.5 per cent of the annual migrant intake. Numbers surged from July 2023. In the two years since then, more than 50,000 Kiwis have arrived annually on a special 444 visa, while fewer than 15,000 departed. It means that New Zealanders as a share of the net migrant intake has increased – from 4.9 per cent in 2022-23, to 8.7 per cent in 2023-24, and 12.5 per cent in 2024-25. Even as the government has lowered arrivals under other temporary visa classes, consistent and uncapped demand from Kiwis has offset these efforts to drive down the net overseas migration rate. The 2024-25 net intake of Kiwis was 30,200 above the 2018-19 level, which is the largest increase in raw numbers during that period of any individual visa class, just above backpackers and students. Students remain the largest migrant group, comprising 32 per cent of the net intake last financial year. But while many of them live in special accommodation, New Zealanders tend to live in the mainstream part of the housing market where supply is strained. But the Australia-New Zealand arrangements would be difficult to reverse for Labor given the close relationship between the nations. Albanese has tasked Burke with finding new ways to cut net migration from 300,000 to 225,000 as Hanson surges off the back of anti-establishment sentiment and voter anger about migration. Treasurer Jim Chalmers used question time on Monday to highlight the sharp trade-offs in the mission to cut back on migration, which Labor is balancing against the need to attract tradies, farmworkers, and doctors. “You can get net overseas migration down as we are doing, at the same time as you can recognise and not diminish the really important role played by migrants in our economy and in our society,” Chalmers said, referencing RBA research showing that migrants were beneficial to the economy. Working holidaymakers have been another area where migration has blown out since the pandemic, this time under Morrison government changes that expanded age eligibility and added a third year visa. Their contribution to NOM in 2024-25 was up 29,400 compared to the pre-pandemic intake. Labor has slowed down backpacker visa processing and quietly paused applications from 24 countries, while the Liberal and National parties have been at odds on backpackers, which are key to Nationals’ agricultural seats. Backpackers made up 17.5 per cent of the net migration figure last year, up from 10 per cent in 2018-19. Former Labor adviser Henry Sherrell on Monday raised the alarm on Australia’s migration program, cautioning that “a few tweaks and some sentimental rhetoric will do little to win hearts and minds.” Sherrell noted that about 30 per cent of people aged 25 to 29 living in Australia were temporary visa holders, underlining the explosion in backpacker and student visas. The researcher called for a cap on population growth stemming from migration of one per cent per year, after Australia’s yearly growth outstripped all similar nations this century. “Without immigration, today’s populists would be impotent. To some, this reality has meant simply ignoring the topic, and attempting to elevate other issues in order to dominate the public debate. This approach is failing. Keeping our heads in the sand will only delay the inevitable backlash,” he said in an article published by Inflection Points. “These people are not racist. A full 46 per cent of overseas-born Australians say that immigration is too high. They are making a judgement about the pace of immigration and whether the system is working for them.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. title: Labor pushes to boost Pacific workers as Joyce says some Australians ‘bung lazy’ - The Age
raw_text: Labor is telling regional businesses to boost their workforces with Pacific migrants as it fights complaints from One Nation and industries who warn their operations will be crippled under government plans to cut thousands of working holidaymakers. Barnaby Joyce on Monday insisted that backpackers should be quarantined from cuts under Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke’s migration changes since they worked jobs that Australians would not perform. “There are a lot of jobs that just cannot be filled with Australians because … they’ve basically risen above the bottom level. Or they’re just bung lazy and are not capable of work,” he said. The fight over working holidaymakers began when Labor quietly paused visa processing in August and escalated this month when Burke unveiled his plan to cut second- and third-year visas by 38,000 places. Young foreigners must complete three months of regional work to qualify for their second visa, and six months for their third, although British backpackers are exempt. The new lottery system for those who want to stay in Australia longer is one way Burke will reduce Australia’s annual migrant intake as Labor comes under public and political pressure to deliver on lower targets. Working holidaymaker numbers have climbed to record highs over the past three years and made up 17.5 per cent of the net migration intake in 2024-25. However, the plan has prompted backlash from tourism, accommodation, commerce and farming peak bodies who say Labor’s plans will deter young people from working in the regions, compromise $1.65 billion in visitor spending and cost 11,000 regional Australian jobs. “The uncertainty created by the ballot is a massive disincentive for backpackers to travel and work in regional Australia,” said Australian Tourism Industry Council chief executive Erin McLeod. Treasurer Jim Chalmers, questioned about the impact on industry on Monday, conceded that construction, the care sector and seasonal parts of the economy were facing worker shortages. However, he insisted that Burke’s plan had the balance right. “We’re managing the migration system in the most responsible way that we can,” he said. “There will continue to be a role for backpackers, for working holidaymakers in the [agriculture] sector and elsewhere. There is, I think, more potential in the PALM Scheme as well for Pacific Island workers.” About 30,000 Pacific Islanders work in regional Australia under the PALM scheme, which remains demand-driven, but some businesses have preferred to employ backpackers because the PALM scheme is more tightly regulated. Burke has also told farmers complaining about worker shortages that they should turn to the PALM scheme, which is mainly geared towards filling gaps in agriculture and meatworks, but also covers tourism, hospitality and aged care. “We have the Pacific Workers Scheme, which is there and waiting,” he said this month. “If they’re [farmers] willing to use the Pacific workers, then everything that they want picked, every job they want done, is completely there and able to be done.” Joyce on Monday said that Labor should be focused on “visa factories” such as universities – not seasonal workers such as working backpackers and Pacific workers. “These people are [in] demand-driven regional areas and give great benefit to our economy. In fact, they’re essential, and you don’t have to change net migration by changing those numbers,” he said on News24. Joyce said the minor party would be able to achieve its own migration plan without touching the 225,000 backpackers who were in the country as of June. After months of confusion over One Nation’s migration policy, Pauline Hanson’s party is saying it would deliver negative migration levels for three years before steadying the annual net intake at 130,000 people, compared to Labor’s 225,000. “You’re going to have an awful lot of people going out, so you still have the capacity for those who need to come in,” Joyce said. Coalition home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam rubbished Joyce’s claim. “I don’t know how you can say you’re going to bring a number down to net zero effectively and say that there will be an entire cohort of visa applicants that will be uncapped,” he said. Still, he said the Coalition would seek to “preserve as much of that [working holidaymaker] cohort as possible” as it finalised its own immigration policy over the next two weeks. The Nationals have also railed against cuts to backpackers in regional jobs. Duniam said the biggest problem with working holidaymakers was the ballooning numbers of UK migrants who have arrived in droves since a Morrison-era free trade agreement waived the requirement for regional work. “You had this massive growth in the number of British backpackers coming to our cities, predominantly not going into the regions and not contributing in the way the scheme was designed,” Duniam said. “So that is something that we’ve had to factor into our policy, and we want to make sure we get the balance right.” He said processing times for visas were a problem. “You’ve got fruit growers on their knees, you’ve got hospitality businesses not far behind them. This is another part of what needs to be addressed in a good comprehensive policy.” Burke this month said the department had started processing visas at a faster pace again. title: Migration fix could hit parliament next week – but these sticking points remain - The Age
raw_text: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor have held talks on migration as Labor seeks a pathway to get its fresh crackdown through the Senate, but the Coalition’s demands on how to crunch the overseas intake means a deal is not yet in sight. If the two major parties can resolve their differences, government sources said Labor’s highly anticipated migration plan could be put to parliament as early as next week. A planned National Press Club speech to announce the policy from Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, which was spectacularly cancelled last month, is unlikely to be the method by which Labor announces measures to reduce the net overseas migration figure from 300,000 to 225,000. Barring any belated change, Labor is expected to reveal its plan in a more low-key manner rather than a set-piece speech, which may create an unwanted sense of theatre as Labor comes under pressure from One Nation and the Coalition after years of overshooting migration targets. Labor is highly unlikely to secure the Greens’ support for any reduction in migration, so Albanese sought a meeting with Taylor in parliament on Wednesday to discuss potential points of agreement. But Coalition sources said the parties remained far apart. Opposition MPs are concerned about any perception that the Coalition would support Labor on migration, which could fuel Pauline Hanson’s talking point on the Labor-Coalition “uni-party”. Labor, under political pressure to act on migration without offending the left and migrant communities, is prepared to use regulation rather than legislation to make as many changes as possible if it cannot secure support in the Senate. It needs either the Greens or Coalition to pass bills as it does not hold a majority. Taylor wrote to Albanese on Wednesday saying Australians had “lost confidence in your government’s ability to protect our borders” and said the net overseas migration figure should be about 50,000 fewer than Labor’s target. He set 10 red lines for any legislation, including making it illegal to repatriate ISIS families; establishing a UK-style safe-country list to stop sham asylum applications; removing legal aid for people appealing visa decisions; restricting access to graduate courses to students seeking in-demand skills; deporting the 77,000 unlawful non-citizens; and turning the Australian Values Statement into a visa condition. This masthead has previously reported that Labor was considering a heavier focus on deportations, visa-hopping, bogus asylum claims, and aligning the international education system more closely with the need of the economy. But Taylor’s hard line on the saga surrounding ISIS brides presents as one potential sticking point that may preclude a deal. Taylor, who is well behind Hanson in the polls, could claim to be controlling the debate on migration if he helped Labor formulate a tough package. But he would open himself up to One Nation criticism that he had gone soft by working with the government in a critical area of policy to conservative voters.

title: French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since spring - The Guardian
raw_text: The French authorities have halted small boats at sea in the Channel on 10 occasions since the spring, officials said on Friday. Despite claims from the Conservatives and Reform that the French were refusing to intervene in small boat crossings, maritime prefect officers were using “intervention tactics” to board or control vessels at sea and take asylum seekers back to France. The disclosure comes as political parties are once again attempting to seize the initiative over small boats over the summer. Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, last week confronted French police on a beach near Boulogne and uploaded footage to X of an officer saying: “Our order is to let them go. We just have to say to them, ‘Don’t do that. It’s dangerous.’” Earlier this week, Reform MP Lee Anderson visited Calais and said the French police were “literally waving these people on to boats”. In an unusual intervention, the director of maritime and small boats at Border Security Command, Charlie Eastaugh, said: “The incidents we have seen in the Channel over the last few weeks are a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting people for profit. It is easy to look at out-of-context images and think little is happening to stop these crossings – this is simply not true. “I know personally how tirelessly French officers have been working to disrupt launches before they reach UK shores. Their efforts include facing violent people with weapons, dispersing huge crowds, arresting smugglers, seizing equipment and collating vital evidence to help our prosecutions.” Every confrontation with asylum seekers was assessed by commanders as well as individual police officers and gendarmes, who were expected to balance the safety of their officers with that of the public, including large groups of often agitated people and gang members, officials said. On Sunday, when Andy Burnham visited HM Coastguard in Dover, Border Force officers had been warned that it was a “red day”, when conditions were calm enough for several small boat crossings. Two small boats attempted to launch from France, but one was intercepted at sea, while the other was halted on land. Small boats crossing the Channel were down by 43% compared with January to mid-July 2025 – from 21,690 people who crossed last year to 12,469 over the same period this year. The drop has come despite hot and dry conditions, which are usually associated with an increase in crossings. UK officials believe that government initiatives to “stop the boats” by financing the French authorities with another £660m in April have disrupted the business model of people smugglers in northern France and reduced the number crossing to the UK. Gangs are adapting their tactics. Boat launches have spread further along the coast, with some leaving from Belgium and others from as far south as Dieppe, a journey of 70 miles (113km) to the UK, compared with the Calais to Dover route of 27 miles. Officials are concerned the trend towards “mega-dinghies” – larger motorised boats – is putting more people at risk. More than 170 migrants were rescued on Tuesday after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire. The sustained drop in crossings was a welcome development for Burnham, allowing him to focus his early weeks in government on setting out his policy agenda. Shabana Mahmood, who Burnham has kept in post as home secretary, has been reluctant to celebrate the recent drop because she is conscious the trend could change if there is an increase in arrivals in the late summer and autumn months.

title: Far-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UK | US immigration - The Guardian
raw_text: Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US after being detained on Thursday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New Orleans in connection with what the agency said was expired authorization to be in the country and a deportation order. Yiannopoulos’s deportation to the UK occurred on Friday, said a statement on Saturday from a spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE. A DHS spokesperson on Friday said that Yiannopoulos, 41, had been arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport. The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”. The spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”. The spokesperson added: “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” Yiannopoulos – who has previously been a vocal supporter of ICE and immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency – was believed to have been arrested while heading to a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West. West performed at New Orleans’s Caesars Superdome on Friday. In 2022, Yiannopoulos worked on West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working for a company of the rapper. Yiannopoulos, a former editor of the conservative media outlet Breitbart News, previously served as an intern for the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene. He eventually became locked into a feud with fellow far-right commentator Laura Loomer, a Trump administration ally who claimed on Friday that she had reported Yiannopoulos to ICE over his immigration status. At the peak of his influence, Yiannopoulos was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency. He fell out of favor in conservative circles after the publication of a video in which he condoned sexual relations with boys as young as 13. Yiannopoulos claimed that his experiences as a victim of teenage sexual abuse gave him license to comment on the subject. He soon resigned as a senior editor at Breitbart. Yiannopoulos was also banned from Twitter, now called X, in 2016 for directing racist and misogynistic tweets against a Black actor in a Ghostbusters remake. His account was reinstated to the platform in 2022 after it was acquired and renamed by multibillionaire Elon Musk. A little more than a year before his detention by ICE, a social media post from Yiannopoulos called on immigration checkpoints to be set up at California “supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersection and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”. He had also sarcastically asked whether it was impolite for one “to masturbate” in public rather than in private “if you are going about your business and find yourself observing an ICE raid” amid the mass deportation campaign that Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency.

title: Albanese Government defends falling house prices as Labor MPs celebrate property market downturn - 7NEWS
raw_text: The Albanese Government has defended falling house prices as a “deliberate result” of its housing policies, as Labor MPs face accusations of celebrating the property market downturn. The political fight over housing affordability intensified after Labor MP Jerome Laxale shared an annotated headline about struggling Sydney sellers, changing an auctioneer’s assessment that conditions were the “worst” he had ever seen to the “best”. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: MPs clash over first home buyer scheme integrity Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today The story detailed a first home buyer couple who secured a two-bedroom Sydney apartment after finding themselves the only bidders at auction. Laxale’s post has sparked controversy, coming just days after Housing Minister Tanya Plibersek declared on Sunrise there had “never been a better time” to be a first home buyer. Labor defends ‘deliberate result’ but opposition not convinced Speaking on Sunrise on Friday, Health Minister Mark Butler defended the government’s position, arguing its housing policies were giving first home buyers a better chance of competing at auctions. He said first home buyers were increasingly taking centre stage at Saturday auctions instead of having to compete with investors benefiting from tax concessions. “That’s a good thing. That’s a deliberate result of the policies that we’ve put in place. We want to see first home buyers able to get into the market easier,” Butler said. He did, however, acknowledge buying a home remained difficult, with property prices still historically high compared to wages. “As a ratio to income, they’re higher than they certainly were when Jane and I were the age of most first home buyers,” he said. “That’s why we’re doing so many things, to help them get a crack at the Australian dream of home ownership,” he said. Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume hit back at the government’s rhetoric, arguing Australians should not be celebrating falling property prices. “Only Labor seems to do this. And you don’t make housing more affordable by making Australians poorer,” Hume said. Hume argued 15 interest rate rises under Labor, combined with rising taxes, had made it harder for Australians to buy a home. Potential first home buyers eligibility loophole sparks concern The clash comes as another key component of the government’s housing strategy, the 5 per cent deposit scheme, faces scrutiny over who can access taxpayer-backed assistance. Economists have urged the government to close a loophole allowing Australian residents who own property overseas to potentially remain eligible for the scheme. Butler defended the scheme, saying applicants were required to declare all their assets, including those held overseas. “If those assets would allow them to put together a deposit of 20 per cent, then they’re not eligible for the scheme,” he said. Hume also took aim at non-citizens accessing the scheme and its use by some buyers who later turn properties into investments. “This is a taxpayer-subsidised scheme. No wonder Labor is running out of money and increasing taxes if they’re using taxpayer money to subsidise what is a failing housing market,” she said. She argued the government instead needed to address housing demand by building more homes and “managing migration” before moving to “fix” the economy by lowering taxes and energy prices. Butler defended allowing permanent residents to access the program, pointing to essential workers such as doctors and nurses who had moved to Australia and were filling critical workforce shortages. Hume maintained taxpayer-funded housing assistance should be reserved for Australian citizens, arguing “citizenship should have its privileges”. Stream free on

title: Housing expert’s verdict after major Adelaide announcement at the former Hampstead Barracks - 7NEWS
raw_text: A plan to build up to 400 homes at Adelaide’s former Hampstead Barracks has drawn praise from housing advocates, though experts say it is unlikely to make a significant dent in the affordability crisis. The federal and state governments on Tuesday unveiled plans to fast-track housing on the inner-north site, with apartments and townhouses planned just 6km from Adelaide’s CBD. WATCH ABOVE: Prime Minister jets into Adelaide to announce new housing estate at old defence base Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said there was “no more important infrastructure than housing” as he announced the proposal alongside Premier Peter Malinauskas. But Gatton Institute researcher Matthew Bowes said Adelaide needed to go much further by allowing more apartments and townhouses throughout established suburbs. “Allowing more townhouses and apartments is key to boosting housing supply, but these kinds of homes shouldn’t just be limited to former defence sites,” Bowes said. “South Australia should be looking to remove the planning restrictions that block well-located homes across its existing suburbs.” The Gatton Institute recently warned that Adelaide has become one of the least affordable housing markets in the country relative to local incomes. According to a recent report by the institute, the city’s house prices have jumped more than 90 per cent since the COVID-19 pandemic, while rents on newly advertised properties have risen by at least 50 per cent since 2020. The report argues Adelaide has allowed less housing growth in its middle suburbs than Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth, despite strong population growth and worsening affordability pressures. Instead, development has largely been pushed to the urban fringe. Bowes said planning rules remained a major barrier to increasing supply in suburbs close to jobs, schools and public transport. Research by the institute found more than 80 per cent of residential land within 30km of Adelaide’s CBD is zoned for low-density housing. “That means most of Adelaide’s residential land simply doesn’t allow for the kinds of entry-level townhouses and smaller homes that are affordable for first-home buyers,” Bowes said. The report calls for three-storey townhouses and apartments to be allowed across residential-zoned land, higher-density developments around major transport hubs and taller apartment buildings in high-demand locations. “Removing these kinds of blockers to new supply would put downward pressure on rents, and help more South Australians into homeownership,” Bowes said. The Hampstead Barracks redevelopment forms part of a nationwide plan to sell surplus defence land. Early concepts for the site include apartment buildings, two and three-storey townhouses and community facilities centred around a large public park. Albanese said the project would deliver much-needed homes in a well-connected location. “It’s this infill development that’s so important,” he said. Malinauskas said increasing housing supply was critical to supporting South Australia’s growing economy. “We’re at full employment, and we’ve got a lot more work that is coming our way, which means we need more workers. But you can’t have more workers without more homes,” he said. The state and federal governments are also investigating future housing opportunities at Keswick Barracks, with defence operations expected to leave the site by 2030. Stream free on

title: Housing market eased 'more than anticipated', RBA says - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The Reserve Bank governor says the world has become more shock-prone in recent years, and the latest oil spike is a complication for the central bank's policy. Michele Bullock told a Sydney function the RBA was "prepared to act as required" to achieve its inflation target "including by increasing the cash rate further if needed". What's next? The Reserve Bank's interest rate-setting board next meets in a fortnight. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock says the world has become more shock-prone in recent years, with the latest spike in oil prices another complication for monetary policy. She said the recurring shocks had been occurring against a backdrop of persistently weak productivity growth in Australia, which had been weighing on real incomes and wages for years already. She warned, with continued weak productivity growth, that Australia's economy would not be capable of growing strongly without putting upward pressure on inflation, and that would limit the choices of policymakers in the coming years. "This is the fundamental challenge for the Australian economy over the next few years," she warned. "When the growth of potential supply is constrained, inflation is higher for any given level of demand, sharpening the trade-off between our dual objectives of price stability and full employment. "In a more uncertain and shock-prone world, navigating those trade-offs has become more challenging for central banks." Ms Bullock said one thing monetary policy could not do was address Australia's slow productivity growth, and while the problem persisted, workers would probably keep experiencing limited growth in real wages. But she said if inflation kept rising from here, the RBA's Monetary Policy Board would be prepared to lift interest rates even higher, if it was necessary to achieve its inflation mandate. She made her comments in her speech to the Anika Foundation in Sydney on Tuesday. The title of her speech was Monetary Policy in an Era of Shocks. Bullock says economy more resilient than in past Ms Bullock's speech was broadly about the similarities and differences between the oil shocks of the 1970s and today's recurring waves of supply shocks. She said thankfully, even though the world had been more shock-prone in recent years, Australia's economy was more resilient than it was in the past, for a few reasons. She said the adoption of a credible inflation target by the RBA in the 1990s had played a "key role" in Australia's improved resilience. Another key difference, she said, was that Australia's economy had become less dependent on oil than it was in the 1970s. "This means a given increase in oil prices has a less direct and less pervasive effect on inflation today than it would have in the 1970s," she said. "[But] this doesn't mean we're immune from adverse supply shocks. They can constrain growth, reduce real incomes and add to inflationary pressures. "In this environment, our job is to keep inflation expectations anchored and make sure that shocks don't lead to lasting increases in inflation. With inflation and capacity pressures already elevated, recent shocks have added further to the inflation impulse. "That is why we tightened monetary policy earlier this year and why we remain focused on returning inflation sustainably to target." Ms Bullock said five months have passed since the United States and Israel began bombing Iran, and since the outbreak of the conflict oil prices have been highly volatile and, as recent days and weeks have demonstrated, conditions can change quickly. "While the effect on fuel prices and headline inflation has so far been smaller than initially feared, headline inflation remained well above target at 4 per cent in May," she said. Housing market weaker than expected, more unemployment needed Staying with the Middle East conflict, she said business confidence in Australia fell sharply at the start of the conflict but has "rebounded somewhat" over recent months. Ms Bullock said the decline in business conditions and capacity utilisation had been less pronounced, while business investment had been stronger than expected, largely driven by investment in data centres. But she said Australia's housing market had been a little weaker than expected in recent months. "We had expected conditions to ease in response to the changed outlook for monetary policy and the rise in the cash rate earlier this year," she said. "But the housing market has eased by more than we had anticipated in May. "This appears to reflect a range of factors, including recent policy developments affecting the housing market, and a general softening in housing market sentiment. "Even so, the easing in established housing prices has so far been modest, following a period of strong growth. "Price declines have been concentrated in the Sydney and Melbourne markets, but prices in these markets remain around where they were before interest rates started to rise in February this year. "Furthermore, the most recent data suggest that, notwithstanding the price falls, negative equity remains very limited, affecting less than 1 per cent of borrowers." Ms Bullock said while the RBA expected property prices to be affected when interest rates rise, monetary policy did not target housing prices. "Rather, what matters for monetary policy is how changes in housing prices affect household spending, investment decisions, and, ultimately, inflation," she said. She said the labour market had also "eased" a bit more than expected in recent months, with the unemployment rate rising a little faster than expected. But even still, she said, the labour market probably needed more unemployment or underemployment to bring inflation back down. "Overall, we continue to assess that some further easing in labour market conditions will likely be required to bring inflation back to target," she said. The national unemployment rate is currently 4.4 per cent. The RBA is forecasting the unemployment rate to be 4.6 per cent by the end of next year. Loading...

title: Why are Sydney house prices falling in some areas, but rising in others? - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The downturn of Sydney's house and unit prices are "less likely" to impact first home buyers, a residential economist says. Data released by Domain shows the city recorded the lowest drop in the country, but mainly in "premium locations". A real estate agent in a traditionally affordable area of Sydney's west says buyer confidence is at "an all-time low". First home buyers are "less likely to be affected" by Sydney's housing price and unit downturn as historically affordable areas have increased, a property expert says. Figures released by real estate company Domain showed a turning point for the city's house prices, which saw the largest drop in the country of 3.3 per cent on the last quarter. Domain's chief residential economist, Nicola Powell, said it was the first quarterly fall in about 3.5 years for house prices, and the first quarterly fall for units. "The fall for house prices in particular was quite sharp. It means that about $60,000 was shaved from the median house price in three months," Dr Powell said. However, she said the downturn had impacted "premium locations" in Sydney's north and east, not necessarily making it easier for first home buyers. "Those areas that are outer suburbs that are much more affordable, these are areas that are actually still rising in price," she said. "At the outer south-west as an example, house prices there are up almost 13 per cent over the past year." 'It ripples out' The quarterly data shows usually affordable suburbs Penrith and Fairfield have seen a $12,000 increase in unit prices compared to last quarter. But, Dr Powell does expect the shift could eventually make it to those traditionally more affordable areas, including Western Sydney. "What you tend to find when Sydney moves into a downturn, what moves first and what sees property prices fall first are the premium locations," she said. "Then what happens over time is it ripples out. It ripples to those middle suburbs and often you tend to find those very outer suburbs either don't see a fall, or if they do see a fall, it's much more marginal." Andrew Partners Real Estate director Gary Attard, who has worked in and around Fairfield for almost three decades, said uncertainty was changing how buyers approached the market. "Buyer confidence is at an all-time low," he said. "We had a combination of the budget announcement, the tax reforms, and obviously with the cost of living at an all-time high, we are seeing the market affected in a negative way." Mr Attard said there was still demand for units due to affordability, but houses and properties with land were "unfortunately still out of reach for a lot of first home buyers". "We're seeing first home buyers hesitant to buy, they're waiting for the bottom-end of the market," he said. "Young first home buyers have got their savings to invest in a property, and that deposit that they initially outlay with falling prices, are scared to lose that." NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson said the change in the market was in its relatively early stages. "I don't want to read too much into it. I still think housing is really expensive in Sydney, so the average house price is still up close to $1.7 million," she said. "When you talk, as I do to people who are on the social housing waiting list, who are looking for affordable housing, they still see house prices as a huge issue." Investors 'sitting on their hands' Dr Powell said a convergence of factors, including three rate hikes this year, had caused the slowdown in one of Australia's most exposed markets. "We've also got ... weak consumer confidence, and when you do see consumer confidence low, it does slow down transactions across the housing market," she said. "It [Sydney] has a higher proportion of investor activity compared to other state and territories and I think what we've got at the moment is the sentiment has changed dramatically." Mr Attard said the investment market in Fairfield had come to a "complete stop". "Investment is not on the radar. Property investors are sitting on their hands," he said. "They're scared to make a move at the moment because of so much uncertainty." Dr Powell said the cash rate had hit its peak, but warned any rate reductions were a "far distance away". "It's important to remember that this is the normal dynamics of a property price cycle," she said. "We have gone through a period of strong growth and you then tend to find a period of weaker growth."

title: More than 1,500 Brisbane children listed as experiencing homelessness - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: New data from Brisbane Zero shows last financial year there were 984 families, including 1,539 children, who were identified by name as experiencing homelessness in the city. The snapshot is used to understand the scale of homelessness in Brisbane, and to recommend ways to improve the situation. Caitlyn Wheatley, a youth ambassador with the Foyer Foundation, reminded people to remember that a person sleeping rough is "someone's someone". More than 70 per cent of families listed by name as experiencing homelessness in Brisbane last year had a single mother as the sole parent, new data shows. Between July 1, 2025 and June 30 this year, 984 families, including 1,539 children, were identified by name as sleeping rough on the city's streets, in parks, in cars, in motels, or in emergency accommodation. Of those families, 715 had a woman as the sole parent. The list of people accessing services is compiled by Brisbane Zero, a group of 32 organisations committed to ending homelessness. The snapshot is used to understand the scale of homelessness in the city, identify gaps in support and track changing needs over time. The data shows the number of families surveyed by Brisbane Zero almost doubled in the last year. Salvation Army Acting Regional Manager Jonathan Dyer described the situation in Brisbane as "quite dire", with the number of children experiencing homelessness particularly alarming. "We know that experiencing homelessness as a young person increases your risk of experiencing homelessness across your life span," he said. "It is all about breaking cyclical homelessness experiences and taking people out of that system into a life where safe and stable housing is a trampoline into everything else that's positive." Of the families recorded, 321 identified as being homeless for the first time, 268 identified as First Nations and 56 had been experiencing homelessness for more than 12 months. Brisbane Zero data shows 318 of the families identified through the list were housed, including 558 children. Of those housed, 41 per cent were in social housing and 35 per cent were in a private rental. During the same period, 2,326 individuals were listed by name as experiencing homelessness, with the number surveyed almost doubling in a year. Of those, 985 were homeless for the first time and 604 identified as First Nations. Micah Projects acting chief executive Bridget Kinch said there were more people with significant health and wellbeing needs. "This reinforces that homelessness isn't just a housing issue," she said. "It takes health, housing and community services working together to make a real difference." The data shows 54 per cent of individuals surveyed had experienced violence within the past year, 52 per cent did not feel safe where they sleep and 23 per cent had interacted with police five or more times in the past year. Since October, fewer individuals have been added to list, however, MrDyer said this did not reflect a drop in those experiencing homelessness. "It means services have less capacity to reach everyone who needs help," he said. "The strength of Brisbane Zero is that organisations don't work in isolation. They share information, coordinate support and focus on getting people housed as quickly as possible." Ms Kinch said the limited availability of rentals and affordable housing was hitting hard. "The cost of living is making it really hard for people to make ends meet so they are moving into homelessness because they can't afford the rent they were paying," she said. Micah Projects was among the organisations to have top-up funding from the state government for its emergency hotel program cut. Ms Kinch said the focus for the organisation, and other services, was on working with transitioning people from hotels to sustainable long-term solutions. "As much as the reduction is a lot to work with at the moment, we are working really closely with the government around that, particularly around housing pathways," she said. Caitlyn Wheatley, who has experienced homelessness and now works as a youth ambassador with the Foyer Foundation, said she would urge people to remember when they see a person sleeping rough that they are "someone's someone". "Every time you see someone out on the street, just remember that is someone's brother, someone's sister, someone's mum, someone's dad," she said "Would you like the world to look at your sibling or your mum like that? "I would tell the world to break the stigma." Want to have your say? Go to www.abc.net.au/yoursay
