title: The suburbs where house sellers want up to $1.75m more than buyer budgets - theage.com.au
raw_text: Australian property buyers are underestimating the cost of properties in coveted areas by up to $1.75 million, new data shows, even as prices drop in the current downturn. Analysis comparing Domain search data to median prices across capital cities from August last year through to the end of July shows buyers are searching at lower price points than sellers are asking for their homes in the same area. The disconnect tended to be widest in inner suburbs, Domain’s Matching Demand Report, released on Thursday, showed. Domain chief residential economist Dr Nicola Powell said she thought there was probably an element of aspiration in searches for sought-after areas, especially in a moment where prices were falling. “You don’t know what you can afford in an area until you actually start doing that research and understanding the market dynamics,” she said. She thought with house prices falling most in prestige areas in Sydney and Melbourne, upsizers were probably looking to see how far their money might go, and finding there was still a reasonable gap between expectations and reality. “This is where you get that nudging effect and being brought back to reality,” she said. “[Buyers] start to look at other property types, and that’s where townhouses and units and apartments really do have a much greater balance between seller and buyer pricing.” House buyers in Sydney’s Eastern Suburbs - North region had the biggest gap between their median search price ($3.5 million) and the actual suburb median of $5.25 million. In Melbourne, house buyers in Bayside, Boroondara and Stonnington were all looking for homes about $1 million below what sellers were asking. Buyers in Perth’s prestigious Cottesloe - Claremont region had a $1.6 million gap between their budgets and sellers’ hopes. Median searches in Brisbane’s Inner Region were $1.2 million under the area’s $2.5 million median listing price. Sydney buyer’s agent Michelle May said houses in prestigious regions – particularly in Sydney – having the largest gap in search and listing prices wasn’t surprising given many Australians browsed real estate listings with no plan to buy. “Who doesn’t love a little bit of property porn, right?” she said. But she thought it also reflected a common experience of dealing with first home buyers, many of whom underestimated the real price of a coveted area, noting the same could be true for sellers in the current market. “I think a lot of vendors overestimate their own property’s value,” she said. “It’s always better than their neighbours’, right? It’s just a natural instinct.” Melbourne buyer’s agent and managing director at Cohen Handler, Nicole Jacobs, said she would have expected people to be searching above the suburb median, rather than below, anticipating discounts on top-tier properties in a falling market. “That shows me that people have decided to be conservative in their budgets and what they’re looking for,” she said, given cost-of-living pressures and potential future rate hikes. “[They’re] hoping that the market has pulled back enough for them to be able to find what they want in that lower bracket.” Across the country, houses in inner ring areas within 10km of the CBD were more likely to see a gap between buyers’ expectations and the listed prices of the homes they were searching for, with Melbourne seeing the second-biggest gap – a $440,000 shortfall from the $1.54 million median listing – after the much tighter Canberra market. Powell said that Melbourne has a large disparity between house prices in coveted inner-ring suburbs and its more approachable outer rings, which was reflected in the bigger gaps. “When you compare it to a market like Sydney, where affordability pressure is really evident across the entire city… Melbourne really is the only [city] that has that strong disconnect,” she said. She thought Melburnians might be waiting to see when and how far “the knife will fall” on houses in prestige areas that have already seen prices tumble up to 20 per cent in the past year. The gap between buyers’ expectations and listed prices for townhouses and units is significantly less across the board, and in most cities there was a greater proportion of regions where searches were either on par with or above the median listing price. PRD chief economist Dr Diaswati Mardiasmo said large gaps between searches and listing prices in the top end of the market reveal how buyers whittle down their preferences as they make the hard decision about what they can actually afford to buy. “[It’s] what I call the sweet spot between want and affordability,” she said, which was driving the gap between buyer and seller prices.

title: Unions unveil plans to extend standard lease agreements and increase public housing amid crisis - 7NEWS
raw_text: Millions of Australian renters could be offered leases of at least two years under a union push to provide greater security amid the housing crisis. The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) will put the proposal to the federal government on Wednesday, calling for a new national standard requiring landlords to offer tenants at least two years of housing security. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Push for two-year rental leases to ease housing crisis Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today The plan would also introduce stronger protections against unfair evictions and rent gouging. Renters would remain free to choose a shorter agreement. Greater security was “really important” for working Australians struggling with rising housing costs, ACTU President Michele O’Neil told Sunrise on Wednesday. “What you need is housing that you can rely on. We’ve got a problem both with affordability as well as security, and a whole lot of workers find housing really stressful and not affordable,” she said. “What we see when leases end is that’s often a time when rents go up, and people having to move constantly makes it really hard to find accommodation near where you work. “Workers need to live close to work. Otherwise, all the money they are earning is getting taken up either in rents or mortgages or in paying for the commute to get to work.” Rents have risen by about 23 per cent over the past five years, while a report released by Anglicare Sydney last year found just 1 per cent of rentals nationwide were affordable for essential workers earning the minimum wage. The proposal comes as “mum-and-dad” property investors face their own financial pressures, with elevated interest rates adding to rising costs. However, O’Neil said the union’s proposed changes were aimed at professional landlords with multiple investment properties rather than people who owned one or two. “What we have seen is changes in the way that the tax system works, which are actually going to benefit people who really want to have housing as a home,” O’Neil said. “Our rental market is dominated by professional landlords. They’re the people who have been making money, and we need to put some tighter controls in so that there’s support for security and to stop rent gouging.” Push for major public housing boost The ACTU is also calling for public housing to account for one in every 10 new homes built, alongside a goal of increasing it to at least 6 per cent of Australia’s total housing stock. The proposed construction rate would represent a fivefold increase from the current level of about one in 50 new homes. “We want to see one in 10 new houses being built being public housing. That means a massive effort from the federal government and the state governments,” O’Neil said. “Having housing in the regions and communities where we need our nurses, teachers and aged care workers to be able to live is a really critical thing that we need to do to support workers.” The proposals follow union calls to increase access to home ownership and its support for capital gains tax and negative gearing changes announced in the federal budget. title: 'It's insane': NT government divides opinion with plan to reduce block sizes - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The Northern Territory government has prepared a legislative amendment to reduce the minimum block size in low-density suburbs from 800 to 450 square metres. Residents say they are concerned for the liveability of local suburbs, while industry and advocacy groups have voiced conditional support for the proposal. What's next? The government will open its amendment to public feedback on Friday. The Northern Territory government has divided public opinion with a proposal to reduce block sizes in suburban areas, paving the way for more homes on smaller plots of land. The proposal will see the minimum block size in low-density residential zones such as Darwin's northern suburbs reduced from 800 to 450 square metres. NT Lands, Planning and Environment Minister Josh Burgoyne this week confirmed an amendment to the Planning Act had been prepared based on the proposal. "Exploring housing diversity, including smaller homes on smaller lots, will help boost housing supply and improve affordability," Mr Burgoyne said. Deputy Opposition Leader Ed Smelt has pushed back on the approach, saying relying on the "ad hoc" decisions of home owners would fail to make a dent in housing supply. "This government doesn't have a plan for affordability or growing our housing stock," Mr Smelt said. "You need to look at activity centres, at transport corridors, at where growth and development is occurring, not going out to our low-density communities and trying to subdivide them." Data from the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council indicated the NT was lagging behind other states and territories in meeting its obligations under the National Housing Accord, with a growing number of housing approvals and a diminishing number of completions over the past year. Locals fear for liveability of suburbs Top End residents have been quick to voice their concerns about the proposal, with many contacting ABC Radio Darwin this week to say they fear the changes could negatively impact the liveability of NT suburbs. "I think it's insane," one caller said. "If you want to live on a minuscule 450 square metre block, they're all out there already in the new suburbs, so why destroy those beautiful old suburbs with their beautiful gardens?" Another caller said: "We live outside; when we have friends over, we entertain outside because we get that beautiful breeze through the garden — if we just build wall-to-wall houses, Darwin won't be that beautiful, tropical, liveable city anymore." Mr Smelt, whose electoral division of Nightcliff is mostly zoned as low-density residential, said he had fielded similar concerns from his constituents. "They love the larger blocks, the trees, the sea breeze, having space around them, that's why people choose to live here," he said. A discussion paper published by the NT Planning Commission indicated that under the changes, home owners could build an additional dwelling on their block, demolish their home and build two new dwellings, or subdivide their house, so long as the new property adhered to the 450 square metre rule. In response to the concerns, Mr Burgoyne emphasised that subdivision was entirely optional. "Our government is creating new opportunities for Territorians who want to subdivide their land — no-one will be forced to subdivide their block," he said. I mean, obviously, building approval is not the same thing as a completed dwelling, but it's a really good sign as to how many completions we're going to get. It's a factor Speaker 3: of demand running above supply, basically. And there are many components of that. Demand is driven mostly by immigration growth because the natural increase that we get from more babies being born, they usually just get put into an existing household. But I think it's more... You know, it's easy to say, oh, like, let's just blame high migration. But I think it's more of a problem that supply is just not high enough. When people talk about people under financial pressure, that people do seem to be still out there spending money on things that we consider to be discretionary, things that they don't necessarily need to buy. So it does mean that there's more errors in the headline inflation figures, but then you sort of get an offset from that by the underlying or the trim mean inflation data, which is meant to look through a lot of the big up and downs, which oil would be one of those. Speaker 3: Yeah, but like the US threatens some rate and then it goes back to a certain point and then it's something a bit lower because of taco, because prices actually go up for consumers. Has the Fed actually got control of inflation? So the interest expense that the government's paying as a share of total GDP is really rising quite quickly. So I think that these moves by the treasury, Scott Besant, will help to sort of flatten yield, to keep them from rising too much further. And maybe one day investors will just say, we don't think that this is a good place to invest. And at the end of the day, I think that this is another, this will give the US debasement trade, which was a bit of a theme last year. I think that that's gonna spruik this type of idea again, that maybe the US dollar is no longer the global safe haven. But I don't think it's super negative for US equities at this stage. Speaker 1: Yeah, well, Kevin Walsh will have the opportunity. The world spotlight will be on him at Jackson Hole, the beautiful Wyoming town later this week. So let's see whether or not he takes the opportunity to give us a better guide on what he thinks is going to happen to interest rates in the US. But as you say, he's been pretty reluctant to give much of a guidance up until now. That is it for today's episode of ABC Business Daily. We will be back with another episode tomorrow. Make sure you're following us on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. And if you'd like to send in a question, you can email abcbusinessdaily at abc.net.au. Diana Mousina, thank you so much for joining us. Speaker 3: Thanks, Carrington, always a pleasure.

I mean, the most recent kind of advertised rents show even much higher rates of asking rents for people trying to get a new property. But is there any evidence that this is starting to moderate and how worried are you about what we're seeing in housing? Speaker 3: There's not really much evidence that it's noticeably moderating, I guess. It's not as high as it was the back end of last year, which is when the RBA really got concerned about it, but it's still elevated, basically. It looks like rental growth is going to grow at 3.5% or so in the next 12 months, which is still pretty elevated. The vacancy rates are still ultra low across most capital cities, sub 1%, basically, which indicates that rental price inflation is still going to be pretty high. I mean, obviously, building approval is not the same thing as a completed dwelling, but it's a really good sign as to how many completions we're going to get. And we just don't have enough completions that are going on. Speaker 1: And that's just because of high immigration, high population growth? Is that what's leading to this mismatch? It's been kind of messy data for the Reserve Bank to look at, because we've had government changes to the fuel excise that have moved in different directions at different points. How big an impact will it have to kind of the global economy? And is there a lesson for Australia, do you think, and how this is playing out for Canada? Has Australia done the right thing maybe by trying to keep a low profile? Well, Speaker 3: we have less to lose because we don't do as much trade with the US as Canada does. It's one of their main trading partners. I sort of think that this won't end up being as bad as it's reported to be because this is the ongoing story with tariffs. Speaker 1: You think it's a taco moment, a Trump always chickens out moment? Speaker 3: Yeah, but like the US threatens some rate and then it goes back to a certain point and then it's something a bit lower because of taco, because prices actually go up for consumers. title: How close Australia is to hitting key target - News.com.au
raw_text: Surge in building approvals fails to close Australia’s growing housing shortage Australia has approved enough homes to outpace population growth, but experts warn the nation remains well short of its ambitious target. Australia has approved enough homes to match its growing population, but more work needs to be done to reach its ambitious National Housing Accord (NHA) target. Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows building approvals soared in the month of June, largely due a spike in apartments. Private sector dwelling excluding houses soared 17.8 per cent in June, although this followed an 11 per cent fall in May. At the same time, private sector house approvals increased by 0.4 per cent to remain above 10,000 houses approved for each of the last six months. Overall building approvals reached their highest levels since August 2021. AMP economist My Bui said building approvals had caught up with population growth. “Despite some softness in 1Q26, recent strength meant almost 205,000 dwellings were approved over the last financial year, up from 189k in 2024-25,” she said. “This is above the roughly 190k dwellings needed to house population growth.” Even though Australia is building more houses it is still well behind its NHA targets. As part of Labor’s response to rising housing costs, the government announced an NHA, a banding together of all levels of governments to build 1.2 million new homes over five years until June 2029. This equates to 240,000 new homes every year. Despite approvals lifting since mid‑2024, on a per capita basis the picture is softer. Only nine dwellings were approved per 1000 people in the 2025‑26 financial year. This is substantially lower than 12 approved per 1000 residents in early 2015 and only a marginal improvement from the eight per 1000 residents in June last year. Ms Bui said the boost in housing approvals wasn’t enough to make up for previous years’ shortcomings. “It is not a particularly large number, given Australia underbuilt relative to population growth between 2022 and 2024,” she said. “And because completions lag approvals due to project abandons and long construction times, it is unlikely we are making much progress in closing the accumulated housing shortage.” Commonwealth Bank associate economist Lucinda Jerogin said cost pressures would weigh on the sector going forward. “Looking ahead, higher interest rates remain a constraint on construction activity, while supply‑chain disruptions associated with the Middle East conflict and broader capacity constraints in the sector pose upside risks to construction costs,” she said. “Although pass-through has been limited to date, the recent escalation in hostilities increases the risk of renewed cost pressure.” Housing Industry Association chief economist Tim Reardon said there was a long lag between changes in market conditions and building approvals. “The impact of rising interest rates, global conflict and tax increases are unlikely to be observed in approvals data until late this year,” Mr Reardon said. More Coverage “While leading indicators of confidence have deteriorated since the budget, and investors are expected to withdraw from the new home building market, this won’t impact approvals for some months yet.” Mr Reardon said more needed to be done to help increase the supply of housing. “Nonetheless, with housing affordability at its worst levels in over 30 years, it is more important than ever that policymakers support housing investment and development by reducing the costs of home building, not increasing them,” he said.

title: Sydney suburbs defying downturn revealed - News.com.au
raw_text: Sydney suburbs defying price downturn revealed While most of Sydney’s property market falls, a handful of suburbs are holding strong or even recording growth. Sydney’s slim pockets of property price growth are now overwhelmingly concentrated in the city’s most affordable outer suburbs, where first-home buyers, newly arrived migrant families and a shrinking pool of investors are competing for homes. PropTrack data reveals median house values increased in just 28 suburbs across Greater Sydney over the past three months, while unit values increased in 72 suburbs, or about 20 per cent of the suburbs with available unit data. MORE: Sydney suburbs with biggest price falls revealed Unit values flatlined in about 11 per cent of the market and fell in 69 per cent of suburbs. Most growth areas were more affordable suburbs still attracting demand from households priced out of the rest of the market. Some suburbs with the greatest quarterly growth included Berkeley Vale (14 per cent), Kincumber (11 per cent) and Thornleigh (8 per cent). B.Invested director and buyer’s agent Nathan Birch said recent tax reforms had split the market, with prices falling across most areas, especially for luxury homes, while continuing to rise in a handful of cheaper suburbs. MORE: ‘Cooked’: Landlords not allowed to rent homes These lower priced suburbs were mostly on the edges of Western Sydney and were continuing to grow because they attracted stiff competition from three major groups, Mr Birch said. One was overseas migrants seeking out homes after getting permanent residency, the other was first-home buyers accessing the government’s 5 per cent deposit scheme, and the remaining demand was from the few investors still actively searching for homes, who were attracted to the higher rental yields available in cheaper areas. “The government reforms have pancaked everyone into the bottom of the market and that’s meant prices for the cheapest properties are rising,” Mr Birch said. Ray White analyst Atom Go Tian said scatters of growth could be explained by a flight to affordability. “The instinct is to assume that when we’re in a downturn it will hit everywhere evenly and this data is evidence that it doesn’t, we know that in times of uncertainty,” he said. “(Buyers’) their ability to borrow is weaker and so they go for these more affordable suburbs,” he said. Downsizers Dale and Lynne Kennedy purchased a penthouse in Castle Hill, a suburb that has seen a 1 per cent rise over the quarter. “Everything is going down and it looks very gloomy for everybody else,” Ms Kennedy said. “I feel we are very fortunate because we’ve made obviously the right decision, our area or Castle Hill area in general has really stayed strong, both in apartments and houses.” According to Ms Kennedy, the market downturn is concerning for first time buyers and retirees. “It hasn’t been favourable for many people or for most people really which is very disappointing,” she said. “Growth wise, it’s a bit of a bloodbath out there. Nothing is selling, nothing’s moving. MORE: 4yo to own Aus home in $25/wk ‘power’ move “People are trying to offload investment properties, which is also concerning and also pushing rental prices up, interest rates going up again, it’s all gloomy and we feel for people either trying to get into the market or trying to even upgrade at this time and sell their homes.” Ms Kennedy said the pair are in a good position. “We are in that position where we managed to sell earlier and purchase our brand new property earlier and we feel that we’ve done very well price wise and location wise.” Properties that are growing in value Suburb/Current median value/ 3-month rise/ Dollar change Beverley Park units $894,082 6% $47,135 Telopea units $740,011 5% $34,277 Kurrajong Heights houses $1,136,439 5% $51,876 Springwood units $805,412 5% $36,624 Woolooware units $1,128,269 5% $50,170 Cambridge Park units $807,904 4% $34,177 Silverdale houses $1,357,815 4% $55,983 North Ryde units $791,960 4% $32,166 Cherrybrook units $1,537,379 4% $62,229 Wyong units $577,947 4% $23,084 Blaxland units $923,553 4% $36,483 Gorokan units $606,317 4% $23,745 Stanhope Gardens units $466,597 4% $17,908 Source: PropTrack AVM, 3-months to July MORE: Striking scenes at Sydney open homes Originally published as Sydney suburbs defying price downturn revealed

title: Radical plan could change renting forever - News.com.au
raw_text: Sydney rent cap: Greens propose new rent control legislation to freeze soaring costs A new push is underway that could fundamentally change the rules of renting in Australia’s dearest city, and not everyone will be pleased. The NSW Greens have pledged to cap rents, with the party arguing soaring housing costs in one of the world’s most expensive cities have left many households choosing between paying the landlord and paying for essentials. The NSW Greens have launched a campaign to introduce rent controls, with Newtown MP Jenny Leong saying the party will aim to introduce the legislation to parliament later this year. The proposal comes as fresh figures show Sydney’s rental market continues to spiral, with house rents in some suburbs surging by more than 40 per cent over the past year. “We want to cap rents,” Ms Leong told news.com.au. “We know that for many households, their rent is by far the biggest chunk out of their weekly budget, yet governments have refused to do anything to regulate it.” Ms Leong said options being canvassed include limiting rent increases to inflation, restricting increases to once a year or preventing increases during fixed-term leases. The party has previously pushed to tie rent increases to the Consumer Price Index and unsuccessfully attempted to freeze rents during the housing crisis. “We’ve given notice of a rent control bill with the intention of starting a conversation,” she said. “We’re asking renters what would actually reduce the financial pressure they’re under.” The consultation is expected to run over the coming months before legislation is introduced around the September or October parliamentary sittings. The push comes against the backdrop of one of Australia’s tightest rental markets. According to Domain’s latest Rent Report, Sydney’s median asking house rent has climbed to a record $850 a week. Some suburbs have experienced even sharper increases. Abbotsford recorded the biggest annual jump for houses, with asking rents soaring 41.3 per cent to a median $1300 a week. Milperra followed with a 29.4 per cent increase, while Monterey rose 28.9 per cent. Forest Lodge, neighbouring Ms Leong’s electorate, saw house rents jump almost 22 per cent over the year. Unit renters have fared little better, with suburbs including Concord West, Enmore and Millers Point recording double-digit increases. For many tenants, Ms Leong said the financial burden was only part of the problem. “There is an underlying stress that exists for every renter in New South Wales when they know they could get an email tomorrow saying their rent is going up by $100 a week,” she said. “People are deciding they’ll just wear the increase because they don’t want to go through the stress of moving again. “They’re sacrificing things like medicine and other essentials to keep a roof over their head.” The proposal has received backing from the Tenants’ Union of NSW, which says requests for help over rent increases have exploded since the pandemic. Policy and Advocacy Manager at the union Eloise Parrab said calls about rent increases had risen from around 700 a year before Covid to about 2500 annually. “Renters are in a really tough situation facing rapid rent rises,” Ms Parrab said. “Unlike other essential services, there are few hardship protections built in. “We do need to consider how we can implement rental price regulation in NSW and Australia to prevent these harmfully fast increases.” She said more renters were falling into housing stress as escalating rents consumed larger shares of household incomes. “Too many are spending too much on rent, with little left over to cover basic necessities,” she said. The pressure is reflected in countless stories being shared by renters online. One NSW renter said their weekly rent had climbed from $500 in 2019 to $750 today. “My weekly wages have not increased $250 in six years,” they wrote. The Greens argue rent regulation is already used elsewhere. “The ACT has a form of rent control,” Ms Leong said. “There are other countries around the world that regulate rents, and we want Sydney to stop being known as one of the most expensive cities in the world to rent in.” She downplayed suggestions the proposal had been inspired by New York mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani’s housing platform, saying the Greens had been advocating rent controls in NSW for almost a decade. “We’ve been fighting for housing justice in Sydney for a very long time,” she said. “We need to create a city for everyone. “The way we do that is by getting rents under control.” More Coverage The party has previously attempted to amend NSW tenancy laws to cap rent increases and also unsuccessfully pushed for a statewide rent freeze. Those Greens attempts were voted down by both Labor and the Coalition. But with Sydney’s rental crisis showing few signs of easing, the debate over whether governments should step in to regulate rents appears set to return to the centre of NSW politics later this year.

title: ‘Thought it was mould’: Silent rental horror making kids sick - News.com.au
raw_text: ‘Thought it was mould’: Silent rental horror making kids sick Tens of thousands of Aussie families could be unknowingly living in toxic homes - and legally, nobody has to tell them before they sign the lease. Families could be unknowingly moving into Queensland rental homes contaminated with methamphetamine residue because there is no legal requirement for landlords to disclose a property’s history to prospective tenants. That’s the warning from Queensland meth decontamination specialist Steve Annells, who says he is called to about two contaminated homes every week and believes many more are slipping through the cracks. Mr Annells, who has specialised in meth decontamination since 2018, said almost every contaminated property he entered had one heartbreaking thing in common. “Ninety-eight per cent have children’s clothes or toys,” he said. “The hardest jobs are when there are kids living there. They’re the vulnerable ones.” One family contacted Mr Annells believing mould was making their son sick. Instead, testing revealed meth contamination throughout the home. “Their 10-year-old had sores over his whole body. His skin looked raw,” he said. “I asked if I could photograph it because people need to understand what this can do.” Mr Annells said meth residue could remain inside a home for up to a decade and that an ordinary bond clean would not remove it. “People think a coat of paint or a bond clean will fix it, but it won’t,” he said. “It has to be chemically neutralised and tested properly.” He said professional remediation typically took about three days and could cost between $10,000 and $30,000, depending on the level of contamination. RELATED: Meth contamination: a hidden hazard that could cost your home As awareness grows, Mr Annells said demand for his services had steadily increased, with properties across southeast Queensland and regional centres including Longreach requiring treatment. He said homes in suburbs including Yarrabilba, Hope Island, Sanctuary Cove, Marsden, Woodridge, Deception Bay and Mitchelton had required decontamination, with four Yarrabilba properties recently referred to him after tenants had already moved in. Mr Annells believes Queensland should follow New Zealand by introducing mandatory testing and a register of contaminated properties. “A watchlist would stop people unknowingly moving into these houses,” he said. “At the moment, if someone chooses to ignore the problem and rent it out anyway, the next family may never know.” Brisbane woman Connie Cicchini claims meth contamination has had a dire impact on her life since she discovered tenants had been smoking meth in her retirement nest egg investment property. Ms Cicchini believed that all she needed to do was get her Zillmere property cleaned, but the contamination kept returning.Ms Cicchini had been letting the property while living with and caring for her ailing father. After his death in February 2023, she had intended to move into the investment property, only to find the methamphetamine contamination had recurred. She could not in good conscience re-let the property and after the third cleaning attempt organised by her insurer NRMA found the contamination had recurred — after a three-year dispute that was eventually decided by the Australian Financial Complaints Authority — the insurer during the dispute resolution process eventually agreed to pay the property’s full insured value. An RTA spokesperson said while Queensland’s Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act did not specifically deal with drug contamination, property owners were responsible for ensuring rental properties were fit to live in, kept in good repair and complied with health and safety standards throughout a tenancy. “The RTA understands the serious nature of alleged drug contamination in a rental property, and the concerns it may raise for all parties about the safety of a tenant’s home and a property owner’s investment,” the spokesperson said. The RTA also confirmed it does not maintain a register or watchlist of meth-contaminated properties and said the Queensland Government was not considering changes to rental laws at this time. Real Estate Institute of Queensland chief executive Antonia Mercorella said there were no laws in Queensland specifically requiring the disclosure of crimes or events that had occurred at a property when it was sold or rented. She said landlords were nevertheless required to ensure rental properties were fit to live in, in good repair and complied with Queensland’s minimum housing standards. “Appropriate remediation works may be deemed necessary,” Ms Mercorella said. title: Sydney, Melbourne in ‘sharpest’ fall on record - News.com.au
raw_text: NAB declares Sydney, Melbourne housing downturn ‘only a third of the way through’ Bank economists warn the pain gripping Sydney and Melbourne property markets is far from over, and it’s about to get worse. Experts at a leading Australian bank have made a grim prediction on the state of the housing downturn in Sydney and Melbourne, declaring it is only a third of the way through. NAB chief economist Sally Auld told an audience at a summit on Monday the “adjustment” to values in the nation’s two biggest cities would “probably take the better part of a year”. “We think we’re about a third of the way through that, both time-wise and also prices,” she said at the event in Melbourne. “We think if you were to take an average dwelling price across the capital cities, it’ll fall about 7 per cent from peak to trough. “Some cities will do a little bit worse, so Sydney and Melbourne will see bigger declines. Other capital cities like Adelaide, Perth and Brisbane, price growth will cool, but they will be relatively better off.” The decline in property prices began to gather pace in February when the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) made its first of three rate hike calls in 2026 amid stubborn inflation. At the time, house prices and buyer activity had been “continuing to pick up”, the RBA’s monetary policy board noted, as Sydney hit a record median peak of $1.76 million. Then the war in Iran, starting at the end of February, added a new level of economic uncertainty which was credited with smashing consumer confidence. Reforms to capital gains tax and negative gearing concessions in the May budget, which were already impacting the market due to widespread media leaks, further evaporated demand from property investors. NAB this month revised its forecasts for 2026 to a position where it saw declines across all capital cities each month to the back half of the year. It has Sydney and Melbourne falling 9 per cent for the calendar year and the combined capital rate at -5 per cent, slashing growth in Brisbane 4 per cent), Perth (8 per cent) and Adelaide (2 per cent). “We expect prices to level out in early 2027 before beginning to grow modestly in H2 2027 as lower rates begin to provide support and sentiment in the market improves,” its August housing monitor report states. Fellow big four bank ANZ this month laid out an even starker future for the national market, forecasting a 10.6 per cent drop across the combined capital cities over the next 18 months. Primara Research has found that would wipe $1.3 trillion from Australia’s total wealth, with about 57 per cent of all household wealth tied up in property. The total value of all dwellings in the country was put at $12.772.6 trillion by the Australian Bureau of Statistics as of the March quarter. Declines are ‘accelerating’ HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham also holds a pessimistic outlook on where the market was headed, writing on Monday he did not see prices rising until at least quarter three 2027. Mr Bloxham said Australia was still only in the “early stages of a slump” and, with interest rate cuts not likely until the second half of next year, “we expect the housing price slump to continue for a number of quarters yet”. “Our central case is that the weakening economy and housing market will see the RBA on hold in coming quarters, although there is some risk of another hike in H2 2026,” he wrote. “We see cuts as quite some time away, not arriving until Q3 2027 in our base case. Cuts are not even part of the discussion at the moment. “Our central case has housing prices falling in coming quarters, with a peak-to-trough decline of 8%, and we see some downside risk to this forecast.” Coolabah Capital’s chief investment officer Christopher Joye estimated on Monday prices in Sydney and Melbourne were falling at a rate of about 1 per cent each month. The man who helped design the Cotality house value index, one of the leading indicators for property prices, wrote on X he expected the downturns in both cities to rank in the top three biggest in their histories. “Sydney and Melbourne dwelling values are now seven to nine months into a correction that is shaping up as one of the sharpest on record,” he said. “Sydney has shed 6.7 per cent from its January 2026 peak, already more than half the total damage of the 2017–19 (−13.0 per cent) and 2022–23 (−12.4 per cent) corrections, and is falling at roughly 1 per cent a month, a pace matched only by the 2022–23 rate-shock episode. “August’s estimated −1.5 per cent marks an acceleration rather than a base. Melbourne is arguably worse: down 6.2 per cent since November 2025, it is already 80 per cent of the way to its 2022–23 trough (−7.9 per cent ) and closing fast on its two deepest modern corrections, 1989–91 (−9.5 per cent) and 2017–19 (−9.7 per cent), while its all-time high remains the March 2022 peak it never regained. “Only Sydney’s 1981–83 slump (−18.1 per cent) stands clearly deeper than where current momentum points. “In short, these are not yet the biggest corrections in history, but on current trajectory both cities will rank among their three worst within months, and neither has shown any sign of finding a floor. “Very hard to imagine how the RBA hikes into this s**tstorm …” Market in phase one of three Nerida Conisbee, the chief economist for real estate firm Ray White, said although Sydney and Melbourne were experiencing significant drops, she did not believe a national crash would occur. Ms Conisbee said values would need to fall for another nine months for national prices to reach a level comparable to a level seen during the Global Financial Crisis. She said Sydney and Melbourne were down 3.4 per cent over the past year, but elsewhere it was a different story. Canberra was down 0.5 per cent for the year, but other capital cities were in positive territory, with Perth up 10.2 per cent, Darwin 13.1 per cent, Adelaide 6.4 per cent and Brisbane 6.3 per cent. “If the downturn continued for another six months, the annual decline would reach around 4.9 per cent,” Ms Conisbee said. “Only if prices kept falling at their recent rate for another nine months, until April 2027, would the annual decline reach 7.9 per cent and become comparable with the Global Financial Crisis. “This is not a forecast. It shows how prolonged the current downturn would need to become to produce a fall of that scale. There are several reasons why I do not expect that to happen.” Ms Conisbee explained the market was in the “first of three phases”, whereby uncertainty over interest rates and tax reforms was keeping buyers on the sidelines. Open home attendances have plummeted to 2.2 people per property and sales are 30 per cent lower than a year ago, she said. She predicted a new phase to begin, however, when it became clear the RBA would not be hiking the cash rate again. “The market does not need an immediate rate cut to improve. Greater certainty around the peak should be enough to bring some buyers back,” Ms Conisbee said. “The third phase will begin when the RBA starts cutting rates, although a recovery is likely to have already begun in at least some markets by then.”

title: Age it’s ‘too old’ to live with parents - News.com.au
raw_text: Half of Gen Z Australians still living at home with parents, HILDA survey finds Stagnating wages and soaring housing costs have turned moving out into a luxury, with half of all young Aussies now living at home with their parents. Half of all young Aussie adults are still living at home with their parents as stagnating wages and ballooning housing costs put the brakes on plans to move out. The latest Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey found 50 per cent of Aussies aged 18 to 29 were now living with their parents, up from 39 per cent in 2001 and 47 per cent in 2012. Want more finance news? Download our new app for even more coverage The Melbourne Institute data is one of the nation’s most important social studies and has annually tracked the lives of more than 17,000 people living in 9000 households since 2001. The latest data was collected in 2024. The biggest change was for those aged 18 to 21, with the number living at home spiking from 69 per cent in 2001 to 85 per cent in 2024. For those in the 22 to 25 age bracket, the number rose from 35 to 48 per cent, while for those between 26 and 29, it went from 17 to 22 per cent. Men were more likely to live with their parents than women, with 55 per cent of younger males living at home compared to 45 per cent of women. Age it’s ‘too old’ to live with parents So how old is “too old” to still be living at home with your parents? Finder surveyed 1010 Aussies in May and found the average person thought 31 was “too old” to still be living at home. Gen Z and Baby Boomers were the least tolerant of the generations, with both age groups putting the cut-off age lower at 30. Millennials and Gen X, on the other hand, thought age 32 was still acceptable to live at home. Finder personal finance expert Sarah Megginson told news.com.au there was still a negative perception and “taboo” around living at home in Australia, despite current cost of living pressures. “There’s a bit of shame attached to it. But in other cultures, multi-generational living is very normal and very accepted, and it’s not a sign that you have failed or that things are not going well for you in the same way,” she said. “It’s got a stigma in Australia.” But Ms Megginson said there had already been a major shift around when it was acceptable to live at home, with all generations surveyed agreeing the cut off was aged 30 and over. “It’s pretty much accepted now that to be living at home in your 20s is completely normal. That is such a generational shift,” she said. “When I think about my mum, who is a Baby Boomer, by the age of 21, she was married, moved out and had three children. You could not get more opposite now.” Ms Megginson said many Baby Boomer parents and grandparents were now seeing the struggles of young Aussies first-hand within their own families. “I think they’re seeing that it’s not the same and that it’s difficult to buy a home and to hit all those same milestones that they did at a younger age,” she said. Housing stress hits high Housing costs have been rising sharply since 2021, with the HILDA report finding 36 per cent of renters and 30 per cent of mortgage holders were now spending more than 30 per cent of their disposable income on housing. HILDA report co-author Professor Roger Wilkins said researchers had seen “big jumps” in the number of people facing housing stress. “In 2024, it affected 23 per cent of private renters across the country, and that number is very similar for those in social housing,” he said. “We’ve seen much smaller shifts for owners with a mortgage, but with 9.6 per cent experiencing housing stress in 2024, it’s the highest proportion it’s been since 2017.” For young Aussie mortgage holders, the number in housing stress has remained relatively stable over the last two decades, ranging from 8.6 per cent in 2001 to 9.9 per cent in 2024 for those in the capitals. That’s despite substantial cost increases, which the report said suggested mortgage entry was now “increasingly restricted to those with higher earnings, substantial savings or access to family wealth”. The picture is “more concerning” for young Aussie renters, with 39.5 per cent spending more than 30 per cent of their income on rent, up from 25.8 per cent in 2001. About 25.3 per cent are in housing stress, up from 17.6 per cent. While employment rates have hit new highs, Prof Wilkins said wages were not keeping up with rising costs. “Our earnings are not rising enough to keep up with the big increases in housing costs and other non-discretionary spending, so the average person is likely to be under more financial pressure,” Prof Wilkins said. The report noted the findings reflected broader patterns of declining homeownership and rising intergenerational wealth inequality in Australia. “Each successive cohort of young adults who leave the parental home faces greater affordability pressures than the one before, and more young adults remain in the parental home for longer,” it said. “Yet remaining in the parental home may come with its own costs, raising the question of whether young adults who leave end up in housing that better meets their needs despite the affordability challenges they face.” Ms Megginson also doesn’t see the trend slowing down anytime soon. “Especially with rents at historical highs … renting in many areas now is just as expensive as having a mortgage,” she said. “It’s so unaffordable that we can see people are going to delay that rent step further and further.” She recommended young Aussies have a time frame and a plan in place, and have open conversations with their parents so everyone is on the same page.

title: ‘Silver lining in plunging house prices - News.com.au
raw_text: Falling house prices could spare mortgage holders from aggressive RBA rate hikes The biggest fall in household wealth in Australian history could be the unlikely shield saving mortgage holders from relentless interest rate pain. Mortgage holders are tipped to be hit by rising interest rates next week, but the sharpest fall in wealth in Australian history may spare them from further interest rate pain. This is due to the “wealth effect” – when prices go up, people feel richer and are more likely to spend. The same applies in reverse – when prices of assets such as housing falls, people feel poorer and spend less money, which takes pressure off inflation. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said the plunge in house prices was doing some of the RBA’s work for it, taking the pressure off further rate hikes. ”Falling house prices is part of the transmission mechanism. So yes, it makes the RBA’s job easier, but it’s by design – that’s the way monetary policy works,” Mr Oliver said. ”It depresses house prices, people feel poorer, and they spend less.” Markets have almost completely priced in a rate hike on September 29 while putting about a 45 per cent chance of a second rate hike in December. There is also a 17 per cent chance of a third rate hike by May 2027. REA Group figures show the housing market has now entered its fifth straight month of decline, down 0.2 per cent in August. National house prices have now dropped 2.7 per cent from peak to trough since March, although they are still up 1.8 per cent over the last year. Experts predict the falls will be more than 10 per cent. Crunching the numbers, Mr Oliver said the RBA’s own analysis showed just how big a drag falling prices could have on spending. ”Each 10 per cent fall in house prices knocks about 0.8 per cent off consumer spending after six months and over a year or more knocks about 1.6 per cent off consumer spending,” he said. ”If it is a 10 per cent fall, then you’re knocking about 1.5 per cent off consumer spending. “Consumer spending normally grows about 2 per cent, but you’ve got a drag coming from the wealth effect and it only grows 0.5 per cent.” Dwarf any other fall in history Modelling from Primara Research using ABS and ANZ data found household wealth is set to be smashed. Based on the modelling, falling property prices will strip $1.3 trillion from household wealth. Currently, national prices sit 3.6 per cent below their March 2026 peak, with ANZ forecasting a national peak-to-trough drop of 10.6 per cent in property prices, with Sydney facing the steepest decline of 14.5 per cent. The fall in value is expected to be 1.89 times bigger than the global financial crisis (GFC) and 2.14 times bigger than the falls when interest rates jumped in 2022. Although, as a share of household wealth, it would be smaller than the GFC, as household wealth has tripled from $6 trillion to $19.2 trillion since then. Primara Research head of research and data Peter Drennan said the size of the shock was unthinkable before 2008. “But property values have roughly tripled since then, so even a smaller percentage fall now adds up to a bigger dollar loss than the GFC ever did,” Mr Drennan said. Not part of our agenda In a grim update for property owners, RBA governor Michele Bullock explicitly ruled out making any interest rate decision that could help or hurt the housing market. “One point to make upfront here, we don’t target housing prices,” she said. “We do observe closely what’s going on in the housing market because it is one area that monetary policy has an impact.” While taking part of the blame for the housing market’s fastest fall in four decades, Ms Bullock said negative gearing and capital gains reforms also stopped investor activity. “You can see very directly the impact of the tax changes because you can see housing approvals for investors have just dropped,” she said. “They’ve dropped for everyone, but they’ve really dropped a long way for investors. More Coverage “It has changed the dynamic for investors whether it’s worth them investing in housing or not.” However, Ms Bullock said house prices had surged since the beginning of Covid and were now coming down from “a very high base”. “At the moment, if you look at how it’s correcting relative to other corrections, and the downturn is sort of in the lower range of downturns in the past, but it’s certainly not out of the ballpark of the sorts of downturns we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

title: Real estate agent’s viral posts show our property market angst - SMH.com.au
raw_text: An inner west Sydney real estate auctioneer with an influencer side-hustle, Tom Panos is someone few would have heard of. But he has become an overnight celebrity and viral sensation after his weekend property post hit the current property zeitgeist bullseye. His weekend post reflected, in equal parts, a sense of panic and desperation for property sellers and caution and disinterest from buyers. Both opportunistic sellers and bargain hunting buyers are populating the sidelines. Panos’ description of the results of last weekend’s auctions he conducted makes for sensational listening – none sold and not even one offer on any of the properties. “I didn’t have a single person register to bid. Do you understand? Not one registration. Not one person even said to themselves, ‘You know what? There’s a few bargains out there. I might go in and just see what’s actually happening’,” the auctioneer said in a video on social media platform X. Panos’ colourful reflections on the market, which he puts on social media sites including X, no doubt help to raise his public profile. However, it is also a sign of the growing property market angst that his posts have gone viral online, while also being picked up on morning television and in other traditional media. It had been the worst he had experienced in 30 years, Panos said. From his position at the coalface of Sydney real estate, Panos reckons some particularly prestige markets in Sydney have already fallen by 20 per cent, while the middle valuation markets are off 10 per cent. He reckons the only category in which prices are rising is at the lower end, where first home buyers are operating. The initial auction clearance rate across the country last week does not necessarily reflect Panos’ experience. At first blush a little more than half of the properties that went under the hammer were sold – although this figure is likely to be revised down. But it’s been 12 weeks now that clearance rates have been well below averages and the negative effect on prices is becoming clearer with each monthly pricing result. Those optimists who subscribe to a short-lived or gentle correction in pricing are looking increasingly isolated. And there is a growing chorus of property experts predicting a rush of fresh housing stock will hit the market in spring and further depress prices. Last week the Australian Property Institute declared its finding that the government’s proposed changes to negative gearing was acting as the largest weight on house prices, even greater than this year’s interest rate rises. And while one shouldn’t subscribe to the school of property price armageddon, it is fair to assume that another interest rate hike of 0.25 percentage points would seal the deal for a decline in national house prices for 2026 that could run into 2027. The good news is that interest rate markets are punting that the Reserve Bank is unlikely to increase rates next month, but the bad news is that markets predict one more rise in interest rates before the end of the year. We will have a clearer picture on how the RBA may be assessing the economic landscape after the June quarterly inflation number is delivered on Wednesday. Inflation is feeding into overall consumer caution as are the twists and turns of President Donald Trump’s Middle Eastern war and its impact on petrol prices. These are not the ingredients for robust economic growth or a vibrant retail sector. Myer’s chief executive this week warned that a sales slump in June and July (that followed a strong May) had already resulted in more promotional activity than had been planned. For the full year to July Myer was expecting sales to limp 0.3 per cent higher. ANZ-Roy Morgan’s measure of Australian consumer confidence fell 4.4 points to 71.2 points last week, which is its lowest since June. This evidence is all pointing in the same direction. And one would have to agree with Panos – that now is not the time to be selling a home. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. title: The tree-change town where house prices have plunged $133,000 - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Home buyers could expect a six-figure discount on a typical property in the charming regional Victorian town of Daylesford, or as much as $400,000 on some top-end homes, as the wider market weakens. Many other parts of the state are pricier than a year ago as investors and first home buyers flock to more affordable options - but those who might have looked for a weekender in Daylesford are pulling back. Buyers are now arriving from NSW, Queensland and SA as the town offers both high amenity and better value. The median house price in Daylesford has fallen by $133,000 since it peaked at $925,000 in the March quarter of 2023, Domain data shows. The typical house there now costs $792,000, a drop of almost 14 per cent from the peak three years ago. Separate figures show it had the third-weakest growth in house prices in regional Victoria over the past five years. Some high-profile Daylesford homes have had hefty price cuts. The town hosted last year’s season of reality renovation TV show The Block, in which contestants transform a house, sell it at auction and pocket any premium over the reserve. The Block airs on Nine, owner of this masthead. Two of the homes failed to sell at auction in October, when they had price guides of $3 million to $3.3 million. title: Why property investors may be buying in the wrong suburbs - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Property investors who bought units in investor-heavy suburbs made a smaller capital gain over the past 16 years than buyers who purchased in areas with more owner-occupiers. Every $100 invested in the unit market in a suburb with a high proportion of owner-occupiers in 2010 would have risen in value to $199 by this year, new research from Cotality found. But that same $100 invested in a suburb with a high proportion of investor-owners would have risen only to $165 over the same time period. The research comes as changes to the tax treatment of property investment announced in the recent federal budget prompt some investors to reconsider their plans. Cotality measured about 3000 suburbs over 16 years and grouped them into four cohorts depending on the proportion of owner-occupiers compared to investor owners in the suburb. The research found that suburbs with a higher share of owner-occupiers generally recorded stronger capital growth over the long term, and the outcome was most pronounced in the unit market. Investor-heavy areas can be more sensitive to changes in sentiment, lending conditions and supply, the researchers said, and developers target investor-heavy suburbs to deliver new apartment towers. Cotality research director Tim Lawless said the apartment sector can have more fluctuations in supply as one new apartment development could add an extra 100 dwellings or more to a suburb. “There probably is an element of a herd mentality – going with the flow and buying where other investors have already purchased,” he said. Investors buying for financial returns react more strongly to price signals than owner-occupiers, while investor purchases tend to pick up when dwelling values rise in a suburb, the report said. But owner-occupiers tend to buy for lifestyle reasons and may be more likely to renovate their home and hold for longer. Owner-occupiers also tend to buy in areas with features such as sought-after public schools or near public transport. Lawless suggested investors chasing capital growth should put themselves into the mindset of an owner-occupier, and look for factors such as liveability, amenity and public transport, which can drive stronger rates of capital growth. But he noted the ratio of owner-occupation was only one of the factors investors should consider – a correlation between owner-occupation and capital growth was not necessarily causation. “Capital gain has always been the main game for investors, especially in markets like Australian housing where yields tend to be extraordinarily low,” he said. “That is going to be changing over time, especially if negative gearing reforms are here to stay – it does imply investors will probably become more cognisant of opportunities for cashflow or the yield of the suburb.” PRD chief economist Dr Diaswati Mardiasmo said buyers may find it more competitive to purchase a unit in owner-occupied areas, bidding against families willing to pay to stay in their preferred suburb. Investors, meanwhile, tend to chase the lowest possible price to support rental returns, even if that means considering a different suburb. She said investor-heavy areas may have recorded comparatively weaker price growth because of the types of units in the area. “When it comes to suburbs with a lot of investors, there’s normally a lot of units in that area to start with, and a lot of the time the units are your standard two-bedroom, two-bathroom unit,” she said. “In owner-occupier suburbs there’s usually a lesser amount of units to start with and the units that are there are not like your tower blocks … usually gentle density units, four storeys, five storeys, where there’s only 15, 20 units in that block.” The research looked at capital gains from 2010 until this year, and did not forecast the future growth prospects for the unit market. The May federal budget’s changes to the tax treatment of capital gains and negatively geared properties may make some investor-heavy markets less attractive, including where buyers have relied on tax benefits or strong future growth assumptions, Cotality said. The report said unit suburbs with a high share of investor-owners face the most concentrated risk and are more sensitive to any pullback in investor activity. Different levels of government have also been trying to improve housing affordability by delivering more supply, including apartments close to public transport. Lawless said supply typically ran counter to the opportunity for capital gains. Any pick-up in housing supply would be “great news” for housing affordability, “but it does imply less upward pressure on housing prices”, he said. “You’d have to expect there’s going to be less capital growth in the market because there’s a better balance between those forces.”

title: Melbourne suburbs where house prices rose – and fell – the most - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Home buyers in Melbourne’s blue chip suburbs can now pick up a relative bargain as the city’s property prices fall, but those looking for their first home in more affordable neighbourhoods may have to pay more. House prices in some ritzy inner-Melbourne hubs fell by double figures over the 12 months to June, Domain’s latest House Price Report, released last week, revealed, while in some outer mortgage belts, prices were on the rise. This soaring outer-suburban market is now making it tougher for first-time buyers to get a foothold, experts say, even as wider house price falls are expected. Toorak recorded the largest decline in Melbourne, a fall of 26.6 per cent over the year to June to a $3.67 million median, Domain data showed, while Balwyn (minus 14 per cent) and South Yarra (minus 11.7 per cent) also fell. That compared to Riddells Creek in the outer north-west, where prices soared 22.5 per cent to $1.09 million. There were also strong rises in Melton (15.8 per cent), Oakleigh South (15.3 per cent), Frankston North and Westmeadows (14.4 per cent each) and Kurunjang (13.9 per cent). Unit prices fell most in Brighton (minus 21 per cent), Fairfield (minus 17.2 per cent) and Melbourne CBD (minus 17 per cent). The middle ring suburb of Chadstone had the largest unit price jump of 29.6 per cent. Overall Melbourne’s house price fell by 3.1 per cent in the June quarter, to a median $1.04 million. Domain chief residential economist Dr Nicola Powell said a shock to the market from rising interest rates and the added cost of living meant high-priced areas were taking the initial hit. “Really, this is the playbook we usually find at the start of a downturn,” Powell said. “Expensive inner and blue-chip areas are feeling the brunt, while the less expensive areas are still holding up.” Suburbs in the middle and outer areas would be hit by the cooling market in coming months, though not all would experience price falls. “A downturn doesn’t mean all suburbs come down in price; it can just mean a slowdown in the pace of their gains,” Powell said. Natalie Weeks, senior mortgage broker with Loan Market Rowville, said first home buyers were finding it more difficult to get a loan as interest rates rose. “From the first home buyers I’ve been working with, they have been finding it a bit more difficult … If they qualify for the 5 per cent deposit scheme, then they do that to help them get a leg up,” Weeks said. Some were relying on the bank of mum and dad, or on family to be a guarantor on a loan, to help them buy their first home, she said. Alicia Alpuim bought her first home, a two-bedroom townhouse, in April. The 29-year-old school counsellor had been looking in Rowville, but found she was priced out of the area. Alpuim settled for nearby Dandenong North, buying close to where she had been living with her parents. She saved for six years for a 20 per cent deposit. House prices in the outer suburb of Rowville rose 8.9 per cent to a $1.12 million median over the year to June, while Dandenong North’s were up 5.9 per cent to $810,000. It had been daunting applying for a mortgage as someone on a single income. “It wasn’t easy at all,” Alpuim said. “I obviously couldn’t afford a house, so a townhouse was the best option for me compared to an apartment.” Alpuim is now weighing up her options of whether to rent out her second bedroom to help cover costs. On the opposite side of the city, first home buyers were still competing with investors, especially interstate buyers looking to invest through self-managed superannuation funds while they were still able, before federal investor tax changes. Barry Plant Melton partner and auctioneer Ned Nikolic said that competition was helping buoy prices in the area. “When Melbourne’s prices fall, Melton’s tend to stabilise,” he said. “Melton’s not going to go down much.” AMP chief economist Dr Shane Oliver said higher interest rates were pushing buyers to look in more affordable areas, adding to competition. “As rates go up, it does make property less affordable, and higher repayments pushes people to the lower end of the market,” Oliver said. Economists, including Oliver, predict house prices will continue to dip through 2026, until there is a cut to interest rates, which is forecast for some time in 2027. “Once the downturn bottoms out then the lower end that held up better won’t see prices go up by as much,” Oliver said.

title: Graya’s co-founder on how to tackle the city’s housing crisis - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city’s most interesting characters on our most iconic form of transport. This week, Graya co-founder and managing director Rob Gray tells us how he thinks the city should tackle the housing crisis, what Brisbane 2032 will mean for construction prices, and the suburbs Graya has its eye on. We meet Gray at Teneriffe ferry stop, just a short walk from his head office. He’s immediately recognisable in a Graya branded T-shirt. As we cruise along the Brisbane River, we spot multiple Graya-branded signs at prime real estate spots in the city’s most affluent areas. What’s your controversial Brisbane opinion? I think, personally, we have a little bit of a housing crisis at the moment. Houses are really expensive; rents are really expensive. What would really help would be going up and not out. Potentially lifting some height limits in the busy areas would really help everybody. In a perfect world, if money wasn’t an object and you could do whatever you want, what would be your dream Brisbane project? This is going to sound corny, but I think the dream Brisbane projects I’m already doing. You know, from riverfront developments in Saint Lucia, to restaurants and retail developments in Racecourse Road and James Street, it’s things that I’ve always wanted to do. Maybe the next thing I really want to be part of is the Brisbane skyline. What inspired you to get into development? From a very young age, I always wanted to get into property development. I just really loved doing things with my hands. I loved creating something. I like the fulfillment, seeing something come out of the ground and be able to experience the hard work. There are whole areas in Brisbane that Graya is really reshaping. Do you feel it’s a big responsibility, and how have you dealt with that? Related Article I think as Graya has matured as a business, I am starting to feel more responsibility to the Brisbane community that we need to do a really good job. Especially now, because we’ve moved out of individual homes and now we’re doing what we like to call lifestyle developments. We like to bring in the retail and fashion and restaurants. It’s putting a huge responsibility on us to make our city great. You’ve had an enormous amount of success in quite a short period of time in what’s very famously a hugely cutthroat industry. What’s the secret behind your success and your rapid growth? It might look like it’s quite quick from the outside in, but for us, it’s been quite slow. But we’ve been really determined from the outset to do a really good product, so we really focused on that for a long period of time. Related Article And you look back over a decade and a half, and you really have done a lot of things. Graya’s got a really distinctive aesthetic and style. How did that come about? Is there a building in Brisbane you’re particularly proud of? I think we’re really fortunate in Brisbane, we’ve got such a good climate – it’s not too cold, it’s not too hot – so we can do this really subtropical architecture. We really like to put greenery within our buildings, and something that I’m really, really proud of is a New Farm building called Mason. It’s on the corner of Moray Street, and it has this draping greenery. Every year it ages, it just gets better and better. Graya’s obviously got its detractors, and you’ve got under the skin of some other developers, among others. Why do you think that is, and how have you dealt with that? I think as we grow as a business, we’re moving into more prominent areas, and in those areas, there’s been a lot of long-standing owners that have, and like it, run a certain way. As we move into these areas, we just need to be really mindful of that previous history and try not to step on too many toes, and respect other people’s opinions and do the best job we can. Is there an upcoming project you’re particularly excited about? We have heaps of upcoming projects that I’m like crazy excited about. There’s one particularly, on James Street, that’s under construction right now called James Place, which is just a phenomenal development. What it will do to Brisbane and James Street is going to be next level, much like what the Calile did to James Street when it was first developed. Are there any suburbs that you’re moving into, or any suburbs that Graya’s really eyeing as future growth areas? Graya has really taken a shine to the Saint Lucia pocket. It’s something that we’ve always known about because we grew up in Indooroopilly and the Chapel Hill area. In the very early days, we spent a lot of time developing the New Farm, inner-city area, but we’ve really highlighted Saint Lucia as somewhere we want to do more and more apartments. With your knowledge of development in Brisbane specifically, how do you see the years leading up to the Olympics and beyond playing out? How do you think Brisbane’s going to change in that time?
